utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, begin the new year by calling your witness. Mr. Nice.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: May I just say two things, Your Honour. First, the Court will recall that in respect of the next two witnesses, the Prosecution raised as a potential argument that there should not be both called, the one being duplicative of the other, and I know that the Chamber has yet to announce any decision on that. The second point that I'd make is that these witnesses are speaking French, and in those circumstances, it will be the Prosecutor who will be cross-examining them. I give notice to that effect.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Nice. We'll take up that question later, the argument that you've raised. Yes, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I call the next witness, Eve Crepin.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Is the witness journeying from France for this? Will the Court Registrar seek to find out what has happened to the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Let the witness make the declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Please sit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: You may proceed, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Ms. Crepin. Could you please tell us about your professional qualifications and activities, but briefly, please. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: EVE CREPIN
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. President. I have a diploma in nursing. It's a vocation I chose. I decided to exercise this profession in the army in order to intervene in humanitarian missions. The whole of my career was dedicated to emergency services and reanimation services. I have also other interests; i.e., literature and history. I have a master's degree in modern literature and I am currently studying history. I have written two books on the former Yugoslavia, and I am currently preparing a paper on the Serb Republic of Krajina.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: How did it come about that you found yourself in the territory of the former Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: EVE CREPIN
utterances.text: I, first of all, worked with the Blue Helmets in Yugoslavia in 1994 in Bosnia and Sarajevo, and a second assignment the same year in Krajina. I then returned on a number of occasions to Croatia and Krajina in Bosnia and Kosovo as a member of a humanitarian association. I committed to work with two humanitarian organisations, one entitled Krajina, founded by Bucan, and the other called Teleobjectif, founded by Marica Mathei. I helped the people as a nurse but I was full aware of the fact that the material aid I was able to provide was totally insufficient and as of 1994 onwards and throughout the year I want to clearly -- I wanted to testify about what I had seen. I therefore took work for two organisations, one which was a K organisation, humanitarian aid organisation, one which was called Krajina, and a number of organisations that were to assess the needs of the people on the ground and -- and write down the statements and testimonies, which is the work I did for Teleobjectif. I also worked for the representative office of the Serb Republic of Krajina. I wrote, as I told you, two books about this, The Serbs in Krajina, and A Testimony on Serbia, and a number of articles also. I also conducted a number of visits with the French television crew FR3, and we prepared a number of reports on Bosnia, a number of information sessions. In France I took part in the Yugoslav central -- cultural centre in the 9th Arrondissement in Paris. I also took part in a number of events in protest against the indifference which people were demonstrating vis-a-vis the suffering of the Serb people, the Serbs being at the time demonised. In the former Yugoslavia, I wanted to testify of a number of the key moments of the war in Serbia, in Croatia and Serbia. In 1994 and 1995, Kosovo, before the NATO strikes in 1998, and Serbia in 1999.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. So you were a member of the UN forces and you joined up in 1994; is that right? And as far as I understand from what you have said, that was not your first involvement within the frameworks of UNPROFOR itself, was it?

utterances.speaker: EVE CREPIN
utterances.text: Yes, you're quite right. I first of all conducted an assignment in Bosnia in 1994 in Sarajevo. I arrived in Sarajevo just after the bombing of the market square, Markale, and the commanding force of UNPROFOR was under the command of General Rose. We were working with the French forces, and we had to take care of sanitation questions on the ground and also we were -- I was running the logistic supply of an orphanage and we had to provide basic materials and they were lacking a lot of these, the basic necessities. I also ensured that the patients were being transported into hospitals and a number of centres, medical centres, that had been set up. So I did take care of the people of Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, please, what made the greatest impression on you during your stay in Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: EVE CREPIN
utterances.text: The attacks of Muslims on UNPROFOR. This had made quite an impression on the military, and we knew that a lot of Blue Helmets had been killed by Muslim snipers, and a lot of military in Sarajevo talked about Serge Verdet and Marot that had been killed in 1992 by Muslim snipers. All the military on the ground knew that these were -- this was sniper fire from the Muslims, and this was covered by the media. And their media deemed that the Serbs were responsible for these killings, but the people on the ground, and given the ballistic expertise that had been carried out, knew that these snipers were Muslim. And the same time, Markale 1 marketplace was due to the Muslims calling to all the officers on the ground and all the military spokesmen on the ground. In the same vein, when I arrived in the BH pocket during my second assignment, the Blue Helmets were quite indignated [sic] by the Muslim sniper fires. In 1994, people had been killed and this had made a marked impression on the soldiers.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Tell me something about your mission now, please, within the frameworks of the Blue Helmets in Krajina. Generally speaking, what were your impressions during your stay in Krajina?

utterances.speaker: EVE CREPIN
utterances.text: In 1994, I worked for the first infantry battalion in the Drina, and I was running the surgical unit or part of the surgical unit. I was working not so much for the French battalion. I did -- I visited a number of people in their villages, and I also took part of the operating -- I worked in the operating theatre in charge of anaesthetics on request of Chinevic [phoen], the doctor. I also took part in all the information meetings organised by UNPROFOR at that time, which meant that I was able to meet a lot of French and other soldiers, and foreign soldiers that had witnessed what had happened in the Medak pocket in 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, please, what do you base your knowledge on about the situation in Krajina at that time?

utterances.speaker: EVE CREPIN
utterances.text: During that time, I moved around a lot. In the whole of the Serb Republic of Krajina and the BH pocket of Bosnia, Velika Kladusa with a friend of Fikret Abdic. I also moved around in the whole of Croatia. I met a lot of Serb refugees from Croatia, a lot of people who had run away from what was happening at the hands of the Croats, and I discussed a number of matters with the military, organised a lot of meetings and who knew the situation in Krajina full well, they knew what was happening and Blank page inserted to ensure the pagination between the English and French transcripts correspond had a lot of information about it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: May I say that the manner in which the evidence is being given is not very helpful to your case. This is a fact witness. You must attempt to focus her on a specific fact situation and try to get evidence that is relevant to your case. She's speaking fairly generally about attacks by Muslims on Serbs, but there is no focus. There is no specific focus. Could you attempt to focus her on some specific fact situation in which she can provide evidence that is relevant to your case.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Robinson, the witness even mentioned the names of some of the French members of the forces there who were killed by the Muslim snipers. Therefore, I assume that that is sufficiently concrete and specific. But yes, I will do my best in keeping with your advice just now to focus my questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, please, what about the population? How did the population of Krajina deal with the difficulties that it was faced with?

utterances.speaker: EVE CREPIN
utterances.text: The Serbs in Krajina were terrorised. They were exhausted. They were discouraged. They had been living for a number of years. They had been experiencing this for a number of years. They were extremely worried about the situation which had worsened over time and they really felt they had been dropped by all and everyone, nobody was coming to help them. And they had -- they all remembered the events of the Second World War which had a play -- been extremely important to them. They talked on a daily basis about the Dinac massacre which had taken place in the Dinac church, and they had been massacred by the Ustasha so they were terrorised about this at Glina. They were extremely worried and exhausted and really felt that they had been dropped by the entire international community.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honours, can I perhaps reinforce the import of what Your Honour said earlier. The witness is, I think, narrating post-event rumour in a general way that simply cannot, in our respectful submission, go to found any part of a judgement. She's simply saying what a number of people said at a certain time, speaking historically. Although there's no rule against hearsay, the Chamber really would, I suspect, require something more particular than that before it could act on the basis of what this witness says.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Nice. I have told Mr. Milosevic that he needs to focus the witness on specific fact situations. It is true that we admit hearsay, but if it is very far removed, then of course the weight to be attached to it will be very, very minimal.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Robinson, I should like to draw your attention to the fact that the witness is not testifying secondhand on the basis of hearsay. She is answering my question about how the population experienced the difficulties, what she saw. So she is, therefore, speaking about the situation, the mood that prevailed, the fears that were there because she saw them personally, and they of course go back to the past as well. But let me more specific and concrete in my next question.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, please, what was it that could have intimated to the population over there that a similar event such as the one that took place in Glina could repeat itself? What might have given them that impression?

utterances.speaker: EVE CREPIN
utterances.text: In 1990 Franjo Tudjman came to power and declared that Pavelic's state was not due to the war but the expression of the secular aspirations of the Croat people. He therefore escalated the events with a view to terrorising the Serbs, and they came back to Zagreb, and they were welcomed and honoured. The Ustasha were honoured. They set up militia gangs in the region which were primarily populated by the Serbs, and those events escalated with a view to primarily to terrorising the Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Did you have a chance of seeing some violence towards the Serbs, violent behaviour towards the Serbs yourself? Did you see it?

utterances.speaker: EVE CREPIN
utterances.text: The Croat people in Zagreb where I went a number of times were extremely aggressive vis-a-vis the Serbs. Also extremely aggressive vis-a-vis the Blue Helmets who were accused of preventing the invasion of Krajina. So our visits were conducted with extreme caution, and we were deemed to be the enemy of the Croat people and preventing the Croats from invading Krajina. So there was a degree of aggressiveness which I could not understand, given the situation in Krajina where Serbs and Croats were living quite happily together.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And what kinds of attacks on the part of the Croats are you talking about? What kind of attacks were they?

utterances.speaker: EVE CREPIN
utterances.text: I'm talking about the 1992, 1993 attacks in Krajina when it was a protected zone by the UN. Biljevaca Square, in June 1992, Ravni Kotor, Rima [phoen] and Zenica in January 1993, and the Medak pocket in September of 1993 where Serbs were tortured and executed by the Croat forces at a time when this region was under UN protection. The Serbs in Krajina, of course, remembered all these massacres. The military discussed this a lot at their meetings, and they were hoping that their presence on the ground would prevent new massacres from occurring, which was not the case, which we would discover a little later.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You worked in the hospital. Can you give us some examples to illustrate the relationship between the non-Serb population in Krajina?

utterances.speaker: EVE CREPIN
utterances.text: First of all, Serbs and Croats were working together as they had been doing for a number of years and as they had been doing before the war. They had changed nothing to their routine. Their mutual friendship had not changed at all since the war. Everybody was working together in the hospital. Everybody was working to help all peoples, whether they be Serb, Croat or Muslims. All patients were taken care of in the same way, in the same professional way, in the same dedication. I remember one day when a pregnant woman, a Muslim woman, used or was given the rest of the blood pockets or stocks that the hospital had left and that was the last we had. I remember that day because the Serbs clearly demonstrated that they were prepared to help all the patients coming into the hospital. A lot of the Muslims from the Bihac pocket came to the hospital, and all were treated in the same way. There was no discrimination in any way vis-a-vis anybody.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Which hospital are you referring to?

utterances.speaker: EVE CREPIN
utterances.text: The Glina Hospital in Krajina.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And how long did you work in that hospital?

utterances.speaker: EVE CREPIN
utterances.text: I worked there for three months when I worked for the Blue Helmets, and then I went back every two to three months for two weeks 'til the Krajina fell in August of 1995. So I literally worked for a long time in that hospital. I was living with the people there. I took part in a lot of things that were happening to them on a day-to-day basis, and I was really experiencing the war like they were at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, please, in view of the fact that you're talking about a long experience there, do you know of any case of discrimination against the non-Serb population or any case in which the Serbs from Krajina expelled a Croat, for instance, or a Muslim, for instance, or anybody who was not a Serb? You lived with the people over there. Can you quote any example along those lines, an example of discrimination that you might have encountered?

utterances.speaker: EVE CREPIN
utterances.text: Never. Never. All what has been said about the hatred of Serbs vis-a-vis non-Serbs is just a lie. I would like to state again that they took care of Croats and Muslims and -- that came from the Bihac pocket in the same way as the Serb patients. Everybody was treated alike. The president, Milan Martic, had given very clear instructions to all police officers: Any act of violence, even a small act of violence, should be severely punished. So the government, the Serb government of the Republic of Krajina, had stated this very clearly. There was no way this kind of event could happen, and I would like to state this again. I never saw anything of that kind. Even in the speeches made by Serbs, I never, never saw even the slightest sign of violence, and their friendship had not been tainted by the war. There were a number of mixed marriages in that region, and the Serbs in Krajina had a lot of friends in the Bihac pocket among the Muslim population, and nothing of that changed. We continued Blank page inserted to ensure the pagination between the English and French transcripts correspond visiting the Bihac pocket to help the friends of Serbs in Krajina and to provide aid -- the aid and attention they needed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, please, when your mission within the Blue Helmets was completed, why did you decide to go back to Krajina? You just mentioned that, I believe. You completed your mission and then you went back. Why?

utterances.speaker: EVE CREPIN
utterances.text: Yes, I did. I spent a number of months working for the Blue Helmets in the Krajina region. I felt that the situation was going to worsen, and the Serbs were being demonised and this was getting worse. When I returned to France, the press, the media covered it in a particular way, saying it was all black and white and the Serbs were in the evil camp, and this is not what I had witnessed in Krajina. The aggressiveness was increasing, and the Blue Helmets had analysed the situation in the same way, and they thought that there would be a imminent attack on the part of the Croats in the Krajina. Also in 1993, a number of attacks had been conducted against the Serbs even though that region was under UN protection. So they were quite prepared for a fresh attack on the part of the Croats. So I decided to go back in order to finish the work I'd started, and I contacted -- there was no humanitarian aid organisation there, and given that the events were worsening, as I have just said, I was convinced that no humanitarian organisation would actually go into that region to help the people, so I contacted the Krajina humanitarian organisation and Teleobjectif, and it is with these people that I went back until August 1995. That I went back to Krajina, I mean.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, please, what were your activities in that period of time, that is to say from June 1994 until August 1995, and in what conditions did you carry out these activities?

utterances.speaker: EVE CREPIN
utterances.text: So from June 1994 to August 1995, I worked on a regular basis in the Glina Hospital, in the operating theatre. I also made several visits as a member of the humanitarian organisation, a hospital in Glina where doctors and staff had been forced to identify the mutilated bodies that had come from the Miljevac plateau. There were a lot of refugees, and I was able to receive the testimony of many refugees and people who had been victims of this abuse. And I made several visits over the whole territory where I was able to discuss with many Serbs about the situation that prevailed and had been prevailing for several years. I really lived with the people there on a daily basis, and I received the testimony of many people, many residents.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And what does that testimony speak of? Everything that you saw yourself too.

utterances.speaker: EVE CREPIN
utterances.text: Well, the testimony spoke about all the abuse of the Croats in the past years and told everything that people had lived before, as early as 1990 or 1991 regarding the refugees coming from Croatia. They had been harassed, they had lost their jobs, they had been thrown out of their flats, they had been forced to leave Croatia. Losing their jobs was not justified in most cases. They received no benefits, no unemployment benefits. They were persecuted and they were really forced to leave Croatia in order never to return. It is true. All the signs of the power, of Tudjman's power, were there. There were all the war criminals. And also in school curriculum, you had new programmes that were introduced, marked by the Ustasha ideology. In Zagreb, street names were changed, like the Square of Fascism became the Square of Great Croats. In the army, Ustasha ranks were taken over, so there were new signs appearing on uniforms of the old chessboard, which was the symbol for the Ustasha regime. All these signs terrorised people because they'd lived through the Second World War, so they were afraid of that reappearing, plus there was all that was done by the Croat forces. Mercep had ruled in a lot of the areas where Serbs lived, so this was really contributing to the terror felt by people. And they were horrified by what they'd seen. The doctors of the Glina Hospital were really horrified by what they saw on the bodies of the people, on the corpses that were brought to the hospital for identification purposes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: How many refugees did you see in Krajina, who came from different areas, that is? How many refugees were there that you saw?

utterances.speaker: EVE CREPIN
utterances.text: I saw scores of refugees. I didn't really count them precisely, but I saw scores of them. About 120.000 came to Krajina. They were not all refugees, but I saw -- I didn't see them all, but I saw scores of them during my visits.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: During your stay in Krajina, you were in contact with Muslim refugees, weren't you? What was the attitude of the authorities and citizens of Krajina like vis-a-vis the Muslim refugees? How many of them were there in the first place, and what was the general attitude towards them?

utterances.speaker: EVE CREPIN
utterances.text: These Muslim refugees had been thrown out of the Bihac pocket during the fighting between Fikret Abdic and the 5th Bosnian Corps. They were faithful to Abdic and they had been welcomed to Krajina between June 1994 and January 1995, and the Krajina Serbs did what they had always done before; they welcomed them, and in spite of the misery they found themselves in. They tried to help these people with medicine, with food, and all the refugees were taken into the Glina Hospital if there was an emergency for surgery or otherwise, there was around-the-clock service. Bread was being served to the refugees around the clock as well, and they were supported for several months without any kind of discrimination. The Serbs did what they had always done before; they supported the Muslims as though these had been Serbs or Croats, without any form of discrimination.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: What is your knowledge concerning the events that are usually called Operation Flash?

utterances.speaker: EVE CREPIN
utterances.text: The Operation Flash took place early May 1995 in Western Slavonia. The Croat forces bombed Pakrac, Okucani and Jasenovac. The people from these towns fled the area to go to Bosnia, and they were bombed as they were going through Stari Gradiska bridge to go to Nova Popola, among other places. They were bombed by the Croats and I met them fleeing as they were fleeing the bombing. These refugees had been terrorised by the bombing and by the high casualties among the civilian population. And I stress this. In May 1995, the Western Slavonia was a UNPA, which did not prevent these people from being bombed. And 5.000 Serbs had to flee through Bosnia, and this did not prevent either the fact that these people, whilst they were fleeing, were bombed. So everything was allowed to happen, and these people had to leave their homes forever, and they were civilians.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. You were among the UN protection force. How come UNPROFOR did not manage to carry through its mission of protection? What did you learn about this from contacts with your own colleagues, members of the French forces or other forces that were within UNPROFOR?

utterances.speaker: EVE CREPIN
utterances.text: In Western Slavonia, the Croat forces blocked the Blue Helmets in their barracks, which meant that the Blue Helmets were unable to protect the population. And in doing so, it was easy to carry out the ethnic cleansing they had planned and to force all these people, all the civilians, to leave, because the forces present on the ground were not able to protect the population due to the force exerted. So the Blue Helmets were unable to protect the civilians.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: What did the Blue Helmets tell you, that is to say, those that you talked to?

utterances.speaker: EVE CREPIN
utterances.text: The Blue Helmets were convinced that this was unfair towards the Serbs. They knew perfectly well that all these operations had been planned in higher circles. They had been organised, and all this could not have been done, the bombing and all the violence could not have been carried out if it had not been decided higher up. And it went on for several years. So the Croat forces could not have continued the ethnic cleansing of the population if it had not been decided and agreed higher up. Of course with the tacit agreement of the international community, which never, never reacted, never did anything.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, where were you during Operation Storm, as it was called, and what is your personal knowledge regarding that particular event? Blank page inserted to ensure the pagination between the English and French transcripts correspond

utterances.speaker: EVE CREPIN
utterances.text: The Operation Storm took place in August 1995. It drove the Krajina Serbs. I was in Banja Luka in Bosnia in order to assess humanitarian needs regarding Western Slavonian refugees because there had been an action in May 1995. Therefore, in August 1995, Krajina was bombed for several days by the Croat army, and 200.000 Serbs from Krajina were driven out. MiG 21s bombed the refugees leaving the country and refugees were victims of stones being thrown at them, and a thousand people died, there were 200.000 people driven out, and in August 1995, the AFP press agencies was taking about 10.000 people who had been reported missing. It was not confirmed, but that was the figure announced then. Houses were bombed, property was seized, property belonging to Serbs, and the Serbs had to leave towards Bosnia in the hope of finding shelter there. There again, the international community failed to do anything. The media did not see anything of the suffering endured by the Serbs. It was absolute silence. And this did not move at all various human rights associations which suddenly forgot what it meant to be a civilian population being bombarded or bombed. So whilst they were protected areas, this bombing, this ethnic cleansing was very quickly forgotten about in the following weeks. I even saw journalists claiming victory during the bombing, forgetting the women, the children, the old people who had died during the bombing. And the 5th Corps, the 5th Muslim Corps had used this opportunity to get into the Krajina territory. Everybody was very happy about this. The civilians being bombed did not move anybody.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You were there at the time, weren't you, and you saw all of this with your very own eyes.

utterances.speaker: EVE CREPIN
utterances.text: Yes. I saw this exodus of the Serbian population with my own eyes. They were on tractors, deprived of everything, in utter terror. They were moving towards Bosnia. I saw the wounded coming as a result of the bombing. Yes, I saw everything.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And what did you do after the fall of Krajina in 1995?

utterances.speaker: EVE CREPIN
utterances.text: After the fall of Krajina in 1995, I continued trying to help the refugees through these humanitarian organisations I mentioned earlier on. I made several visits to Bosnia, to Kosovo, and to the rest of Serbia in refugee camps, in hospitals, there where they might have been evacuated. As of August 1995, I went to some regions in Bosnia. I went to Banja Luka, Prijedor, Derventa, Brcko, Bijeljina. In Eastern Bosnia I went to Pale, Zvornik, Bratunac and Srebrenica because I was on the lookout for refugees. I met church authorities and political authorities who might have been able to help me assess the humanitarian needs of the Serb population, of all these refugees. I met with Mr. Pavle, I met with President Martic, with Karadzic, with Mladic, and later on with Mrs. Plavsic and Mr. Krajisnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You mentioned many towns that you were in. Tell us briefly, what was the position of the population like, the population that you saw in Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: EVE CREPIN
utterances.text: The Serb population in Bosnia was suffering from the war. This embargo had been imposed on the area, and this could be felt in everyday life. Everything was missing. Basic commodities were missing. There were no hygiene products, which was a real problem for hospitals. It was therefore difficult for hospitals to operate properly. They did not have any pain-killers, any anaesthetics, any medicine. There was no work. There was no money, basically. And the most tragic thing is that there was no humanitarian aid. All these people were abandoned and they knew that they were demonised. They knew that too, and they were very worried about their future because they knew this demonisation was responsible for the lack of humanitarian aid and that the situation was not likely to get any better for them. Of course, psychologically speaking, they were very hit by the war as is true of any population, because most families had lost children, relatives, brothers and sisters. They had been separated. Many did not know anything about the fate of their relatives. So it was the Serb population suffering as any population suffers during the war. But that was not said by the media. That was quite obvious. If you worked in the field with the population, you noticed that very clearly.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You mentioned the media a few times. Tell me, what is your impression regarding the writing of the media? For example, in France or the Western media in general, those that you followed. I mean their attitude towards the reality that you saw with your own eyes throughout this period of time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, the question that you just asked is indicative of the problem with this evidence, this kind of evidence. "What is your impression regarding the writing of the media?" The witness is really giving impressions, and we are not particularly concerned with general impressions. And so I would like you to try to focus the witness, if it is possible, on something which is beyond general impressions, because general impressions are not very helpful.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The witness mentioned that the media did not attach any -- did not pay any attention whatsoever to the crimes that were committed against the Serbs. And these were mass crimes at that. So I asked her how this was portrayed in the media, I mean the reality that she saw with her very own eyes where she lived and worked. She's a humanitarian aid worker. She was on the spot, she met thousands of people, she worked in hospitals, helped there; she was a participant in all these events. On the other hand, she said a few minutes ago that she saw that the Western media kept quiet about this.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So my question is: What is the balance between the situation on the ground and the writing of the media on the other hand?

utterances.speaker: EVE CREPIN
utterances.text: These are not impressions. That was stated by the media, by the press. The media were very simple. It was a black and white presentation with two sides; the evil one, the Serb aggressor that had unleashed the war, according to the media. And the media were very clear the Serbs did not suffer from the war; there were no refugees, there were no detention camps for the Serbs. And then on the other side, on the good side, you had all the victims, therefore all the other ethnic groups, the Croats, the Muslims. That was a very black and white presentation. And all press news was saying that -- denying any suffering by the Serbs, by the civilian population in refugee camps, in detention camps, denying any torture, and you had populations that were the victims of these barbaric Serbs that were throat-cutters and criminals. So starting on this basis, the most enormous lies were propagated by the press, by the media, without any people questioning it, and there was utter silence as to the suffering by the Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, did you learn anything about the fate of the Serbs who found themselves in Croat prisons? If you have any such knowledge, what is it?

utterances.speaker: EVE CREPIN
utterances.text: I met families who had some of their relatives gaoled in Croat prisons. There were scores of detention camps created in Croatia as early as in 1991. In Western Slavonia, for instance, in October 1991 already Serbs were executed. In Marino Selo and Pakracka Poljana next to Marino Selo, detention camps were set up. There was Stara Ciglana in Pakracka Poljana and Rivaska Poljana [phoen] in Marino Selo. In those camps, hundreds of Serbs were detained, mistreated and tortured. Also in the Lora camp in Split already in 1992 and until 1997, thousands of Serbs were detained. Journalists, some journalists wrote a lot about this prison, and some 70 people died, according to them, in the camp. All the UN officials, International Red Cross, other humanitarian organisations knew of those camps but nothing was done, obviously. Toni Manic [phoen], who is now the president of Human Rights in Dalmatia worked a lot with the Veritas organisation from Belgrade but also with Vojin Babic, who did a lot about the camps, and they gave a lot of evidence regarding the victims to the ICTY, with autopsy reports in order Blank page inserted to ensure the pagination between the English and French transcripts correspond to show that those camps had existed and that there were victims who were mistreated in those camps. I also want to stress that regarding the Lora camp, the ICTY had the files, but the former guards of the camp were not prosecuted by the ICTY. They were prosecuted and tried by the Croat system in Split, and they were all acquitted.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, in Krajina you saw many Serb refugees and many Muslim refugees, isn't that right? Where did all these refugees come from?

utterances.speaker: EVE CREPIN
utterances.text: Many of refugees from Croatia had been driven out as early as in 1990 or 1991. I told you that Serbs had been harassed, humiliated, and driven out of their homes, and they suffered from the special forces of the MUP, especially the forces under Tomislav Mercep. In Eastern Slavonia, the Serbs had to leave their homes already in April 1991 because in some villages the Croat mayors had put notice on all the Serb homes saying that they had to leave within the next 48 hours without taking anything with them. Those who didn't want to go away, to leave, were put in gaol. And everybody, all of them suffered from such measures because they had to leave their homes without any money, without any property. And a lot of them went towards Krajina where there was already a majority of Serbs. Already during summer 1992, in Zagreb and the surrounding area, in areas where there was a majority of Serbs, the Serbs had to leave and sought refuge in Krajina.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I can't help but observe, although the point can be made in cross-examination, that this is -- these are events years before this witness was ever on the territory that she's speaking about, and the value to the Chamber is, in our respectful submission, limited or nil.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, you heard that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Milosevic, much of this evidence I don't think we will be able to attach much weight to it. The case is not about Serb detention or Serb deaths unless Serb deaths or Serb detention is specifically related to one of the charges. Otherwise, you open yourself up to the submission that it is tu quoque evidence, which is not -- which is not relevant. I haven't stopped you because some of the evidence, arguably, is relevant, and I want to be absolutely fair to you, but I must say that much of it is bordering on not being very helpful to the Chamber. And I hope that this is not an example of the way your fact witnesses will testify. And much of it comes across like a conversation over a cup of tea on a veranda, and I don't find it very helpful but I haven't stopped you because it is related in a general way to the case, but I don't think that you will derive much help from evidence of this kind. And we will have to address the question raised by the Prosecutor in relation to the other witness if the evidence will be of this kind.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Robinson, Mr. Nice's comment is not in order, because the fact that somebody became a refugee before the witness came to Krajina does not mean that the witness, once she arrived, did not come across and find those refugees and was not able to establish how those refugees came to be there in the first place. So she is testifying not about the events that took place before, but she is mentioning the causes of this phenomenon that she witnessed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I did not support Mr. Nice's comment. My comment was quite independent of that.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I didn't hear that part. Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You were in Kosovo a little before the NATO bombing took place there. What was the situation like during that period of time when you arrived in Kosovo? Could you give us a brief description of what you found when you arrived.

utterances.speaker: EVE CREPIN
utterances.text: Yes. I was in Kosovo in 1998, where I spent a lot of time in Pristina and Pec. The atmosphere there was particularly tense. As in Pristina it was quite impossible for Serbs and Westerners who might have been suspected of helping Serbs to move around freely. In Pec it was easier to move around during the day, but at night it was not recommended to move around and leave your house. So the situation was particularly tense vis-a-vis the Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And how long did you spend in Pristina and Pec? During what period? When were you there?

utterances.speaker: EVE CREPIN
utterances.text: I went to Pristina in June of 1998 where I met Popovic, the dean, who strongly advised me not to go to Pec because the KLA was blocking the roads and had organised war operations. In 1998 I worked a number of months in the hospital of Pec. I had got to know about the situation in Kosovo at that time and I wanted to help as I was a professional nurse, so I contacted the Orthodox church. Their members were the only people who could move about freely in the region. I met the Patriarch Pavle who gave me a letter so that I could go to Pec. So I went to Pec and, given the fighting at the hands of the KLA, there were a number of injured people that needed to be attended to.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, what was the situation like in the Pec hospital?

utterances.speaker: EVE CREPIN
utterances.text: The Glina and the Pec hospital likewise, the communities were working together. There were a lot of Albanian nurses and doctors in the hospital. Everybody was working together, and everybody was working together in the same way with the wounded, whether they be Serb or Albanian. They were -- had close ties and there were no particular tensions, and it was all very friendly.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So in Pec, in the hospital there, there were doctors and nurses working there who were Serbs, Albanians, and others, too. That's what you yourself saw, is it; is that right?

utterances.speaker: EVE CREPIN
utterances.text: Yes, that's quite right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Now, when it comes to the patients themselves, were there any wounded among the patients; and if so, who were they wounded by? What did you learn about that, in view of the fact that you worked there throughout? What insight did you have into things like that?

utterances.speaker: EVE CREPIN
utterances.text: There were a lot of injured people coming in and a number of Serb victims who had been injured by the KLA. Injuries: They had been burnt, they had had bullet wounds, and there were a number of Albanian patients. These were moderate Albanians who had been beaten up by the KLA people and also sometimes because they were just simply friendly with the Serbs. So they had bruises, they had broken limbs, and these people had been beaten up by the KLA militia.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Tell me --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Ms. Crepin, were there any Muslim patients who were victims of Serb violence?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Never. I never saw a single Muslim having been injured by a Serb. The Muslims who came into the hospital had been injured by the KLA militia, and the KLA militia also attacked some of the Albanian civilians because they were close to the Serbs. I never saw a single Muslim being attacked by a Serb. There was no hatred of Serbs vis-a-vis Albanians, contrary to what has been said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: How were you able to ascertain that the Muslim patients had been attacked by the KLA?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Because that's what they said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Since you were both in Pec and Pristina, tell me, please, what about the presence of the police in those two towns, the ones you were in? They're large towns after all, both Pristina and Pec. So were the police there? What was the police presence like there?

utterances.speaker: EVE CREPIN
utterances.text: What was quite striking was that in Pec and in Pristina alike, the presence of the police or the military was no more important than elsewhere. In Paris, for instance. If you remember the Vigie Pirate in Paris, which had been set up in order to forestall terrorist attacks. Blank page inserted to ensure the pagination between the English and French transcripts correspond Police presence was no greater than in Paris at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And what was your experience with regard to international relations in Pec, for example? Because you spent a relatively long time working in the hospital, you worked with the doctors of different ethnic groups and with patients of different nationalities, so what would be your impressions of the attitude and relationship between the different ethnic groups in Pec?

utterances.speaker: EVE CREPIN
utterances.text: In the hospital itself, there was no problem whatsoever between the Serbs and the Albanians any more than in Glina where medical care and surgical intervention protected us from that kind of thing. However, in the streets and the shops of Pec, the Albanians were very aggressive towards the Serbs, where the Serbs were not, conversely. And the Albanians were, which was quite surprising because, according to what I saw and after the number of weeks I spent there, the Albanians were living in quite satisfactory conditions without suffering from any kind of discrimination. They were not fired from any administrative jobs. They were running most of the shops. But there was a lot of underlying aggression, and when I spoke in Serb, people picked me up on that one and I was told that in Kosovo one spoke Albanian and not Serb. So the violence was really directed at the Serbs and they were very worried about it because this materialised in a number of ways. Sometimes acts of physical violence. The Serbs were living quite happily with the Albanians, but Albanians were very aggressive and this was very difficult to understand for the Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: In either Pec or Pristina, throughout the time you were there, did you ever see any police intervention or the army intervening against the Albanians, for example?

utterances.speaker: EVE CREPIN
utterances.text: Never. I never saw any mistreatment, arrest either from the Serb military or the police. I never saw mistreatment at the hand of Serbs vis-a-vis the Albanians, never, during all the time of my -- during the time of my stay there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And did you see any violence on the part of the Albanian militants towards the Serbs, for instance, during your stay in Pec and in Pristina?

utterances.speaker: EVE CREPIN
utterances.text: In the streets, one could not see any physical violence per se. I could sense the aggressiveness. I saw physical violence in the hospital itself when the Serbs came in and were brought in and were injured, but in the street I could only sense the aggressiveness. I never actually saw an act of violence in the street.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: In Kosovo and Metohija, were you able to see some refugees from Krajina, for example? Did you ever see them, ones that you had previously been in contact with while you were in Krajina?

utterances.speaker: EVE CREPIN
utterances.text: Pec -- in Pec during the offensive of 1994, a refugee camp for the Serbs in Krajina had been set up. I met these people, and like all the other Serb refugees, they were suffered from shortage of all and everything and had received no aid, had no money, and survived in these refugee camps. They were often attacked by the KLA terrorists. This is what they feared first and foremost. They wanted to leave Kosovo but didn't have enough money and had no visas, and nobody was prepared to welcome them in Europe, so they literally could not leave these refugee camps where they were only struggling to survive.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You were in Serbia during the bombing, the NATO bombing. What period of time were you in Serbia actually?

utterances.speaker: EVE CREPIN
utterances.text: I was in Serbia in March and April of 1999. During the NATO bombing campaign, there were tens of thousands of bombs that fell on the town. There were a lot of collateral -- there was a lot of collateral damage. That's how it was coined at the time. A lot of residential areas and homes were shelled and they were responsible for the deaths of civilians where, in the building of Serb television, 16 television crew died, and a lot of industrial sites and petrochemical -- Novi Sad, Kragujevac, these industrial sites were completely destroyed and had very adverse effects for the neighbouring population because the whole area as a result of this is polluted. The groundwater tables, the ground, everything was polluted and this has adverse effects on the population. If the region -- I personally believe that this bombing campaign which was decided in the name of human rights, in the name of freedom and the name of democracy are war crimes and crimes against humanity. They first and foremost hit or targeted civilians.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Ms. Crepin, we don't need to hear that from you. We'll make our own determination about the nature of the crimes. Yes, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Ms. Crepin, you said you were in Pristina in June 1998, and when was it you stayed in Pec? Because you said you were in Serbia in March 1999. So you stayed the whole period in between in Pec, or can you identify the period you stayed in Pec?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I was in Pristina in June of 1998, and in Pec during the summer of 1998.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: "Summer" meaning? Could you identify the months. How long did you stay there; from when until when, in Pec?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In July and August of 1998.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Kwon.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Now, you were an eyewitness of the exodus of the Serbs from Krajina, and you were also an eyewitness to the exodus of the Serbs from Kosovo in 1999; right?

utterances.speaker: EVE CREPIN
utterances.text: Yes, you're quite right. Let me remind you that at this time the Serbs were victims of this massive exodus in Krajina where 200.000 Serbs were driven out of their homes in a few days. The second exodus in Kosovo. But I'd like to remind you that the NATO bombing campaign caused the exodus of approximately 1 million people. 800.000 Albanian people had to flee their homes, and 200.000 Roma and Gypsies had to run away from the NATO bombing. Most of them returned to Kosovo, but -- so a lot of them have returned, but in total over 400.000 Serbs in Yugoslavia were driven out of their homes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: During your activities, you had contacts with non-governmental organisations, I take it. Can you tell us something about your experience about the activities engaged in by the non-governmental organisations. Or, rather, let me be more specific: Did you come into contact with Western non-governmental organisations?

utterances.speaker: EVE CREPIN
utterances.text: No, I never met any Western NGO. Most Western NGOs worked for the Croats and the Muslims. In 1992 and 1993, Medecins du Monde launched a campaign against the Serbs and against you, Mr. Milosevic, where you had been compared to Hitler. And Medecins du Monde then helped the Croat population in Dubrovnik. Medecins sans Frontieres went to Vukovar to provide relief there to the population, and I did not meet any NGO on the side of the Serbs. In Bosnia, likewise, the Western NGOs did not even mention the suffering of the Serbs, and for obvious reasons, because they were not helping them. The NGOs were only helping the Muslims and the Croats in Eastern Bosnia where they provided relief to Muslim population in Gorazde and Zepa, and they exaggerated the suffering of the Muslims. Not that I'm saying this wasn't the case, but I'd just like to stress the fact that they exaggerated this, talked about cannibalism, famine in these pockets, that hospitals were overwhelmed by the number of people coming in. And when we went to visit these enclaves, we realised that all and everything had been said. Of course it was -- there was a war, but people were not dying of hunger and the streets were not full of corpses. In the same way, Medecins sans Frontieres exerted a lot of pressure, so -- for a parliamentary commission to take -- to deal with the Srebrenica question. In Kosovo, Medecins du Monde released witness reports or -- on the number of refugees and casualties which were the way of substantiating the bombing campaign, and Medecins du Monde was MSF International -- MSF France was in Greece, worked in Greece but was not entitled to work with MSF International because they had helped the Serbs. So during this entire war, the Serbs were never helped by any Blank page inserted to ensure the pagination between the English and French transcripts correspond Western NGO of any kind.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. So not a single Western NGO, non-governmental organisation, during all that suffering, came to the assistance of the Serbs. Who did help the Serbs, then, from your experience?

utterances.speaker: EVE CREPIN
utterances.text: Well, even today the Orthodox dioceses, which is humanitarian aid which was run by Marica Mathei, that always helped the Serb population without actually talking about it and doing as much as she could to help the Serb people. As there was an embargo placed on Serbia, these people did all they could to help the refugees and the injured people but it was very difficult to provide relief to all and everyone because they were lacking a lot of resources. So the dioceses tried to help these people as best they could. The Yugoslav Red Cross also helped the Serbs but did not have the same resources as Medecins du Monde or Medecins sans Frontieres in the Krajina which had been created by Bucan that is no longer in existence did help the Serbs in Krajina for a number of years. There were a number of volunteers working from them. Serbs from France and Friends were providing help to these people. The International Red Cross has been helping the refugees in Serbia and Montenegro since the end of the bombing campaign. But in 2002 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I'm stopping you on that. I think we have heard enough, and I'm not satisfied that the question as to who helped the Serbs is relevant to any of the charges. So please ask another question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Ms. Crepin, you said earlier that NATO bombing caused the exodus of approximately 1 million people. I expected Mr. Milosevic to elaborate on that issue, but he didn't, so I'm asking -- I have to ask this. What is your basis for that assertion, first in terms of number, and second, the cause of the exodus? Did you get the question?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You are asking me, if I've understood you correctly, what enables me to state these figures and the reason for the exodus; is that right?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. How are you able to ascertain the cause of the refugees moving out, the cause of the exodus, and what is your basis for that number, 1 million people?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As far as the reasons are concerned, I base my assertion on the report which was drafted by the OSCE as of October 1998 onwards. An observation mission, KVM, was set up in Kosovo, and they left Kosovo in March 1999, a few days before the NATO bombing. This is a report in two volumes which quite clearly explains that no ethnic cleansing had taken place before the bombing campaign, and the exodus and mistreatments started at the time of the bombing. So the report is very clear on this particular point. This is the OSCE report which was published at the end of 1999. Now, as far as the figures I quoted, I base my assertion on all the reports provided by the International Red Cross, UNHCR, and these figures have not been challenged by anybody so far.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So the cause, as you understand it, is sort of an assumption or guess on your part? What you are saying is that because there is no mention of -- I'm not sure about that, but there's no mention of ethnic cleansing or the discrimination before the NATO bombing began, so the cause should be the NATO bombing? Am I right in so understanding?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, not at all. I quote the OSCE report. So this is not an impression or my understanding of this. I base this on the OSCE report. The exodus started when the bombing started, and the observation mission of the OSCE, there was no ethnic cleansing or violence before. I'm just quoting the OSCE report, and I'm not interpreting this in any way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: That will be pursued by the Prosecutor later, I see. Please proceed, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Ms. Crepin, I know that you went back to Yugoslavia after the bombing, that you returned, and you mentioned members of the non-Albanian minorities in Kosovo, and as a member of various humanitarian organisations, did you have a personal insight into the situation of those members of non-Albanian communities in Kosovo and Metohija?

utterances.speaker: EVE CREPIN
utterances.text: Yes. You're quite right. The non-Albanian minorities in Kosovo for a number of years now since the end of the bombing have been the target of attacks and humiliation. Most Albanians have returned to Kosovo after the bombings, but to date only 3 per cent of the minority groups or members of these minority groups have returned to Kosovo. A lot have gone back to see what was happening there. Samir Rifati, Voice of Roma, who is in charge of the Roma refugees around the world was shocked when he saw the gap that existed between what he saw on the ground and what the international community was saying. The international community was proud of setting up an interethnic community, but the Romas were still having to leave their houses and were still being attacked by the Albanians. Their homes have been destroyed, they had to flee their homes, so those people that have stayed, all those who have returned, are living in enclaves, receiving a small stipend from the UN, and nothing has been done, neither by Munich or KFOR to protect this group of people. So much for the fate of the Romas in Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And finally, tell me just this, please: Are you referring to the Romas or do you include there the Serbs, Montenegrins, and other non-Albanian communities in Kosovo and Metohija?

utterances.speaker: EVE CREPIN
utterances.text: I talked about the Romas, but the Serbs are in exactly the same situation. Since June 1999 when KFOR entered that territory, the Serbs are living in fear. Since the end of the bombing and the setting up of KFOR and UNMIK --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: I didn't hear the figure, somebody coughed, I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- thousand five hundred people were injured and one million people had been abducted. Tens of thousands of acts of violence vis-a-vis the Serbs, 50.000 homes have been burnt, a hundred or so monasteries have been destroyed, and a lot of Albanians have returned to Kosovo, attracted by the trafficking which is currently taking place. UNMIK and KFOR are currently powerless vis-a-vis the situation. March 1994 was -- clearly testified this absence of protection and violence against in March 2004, JJP, where they say that UNMIK is not responsible for not protecting the Serbs. And they also say that UNMIK is responsible for the lack of protection. For the time being, the Serbs are not being protected, and a few Serbs are coming back to Kosovo. It's important to know that the protection of Kosovo mission comprises a number of Albanians, a lot of KLA members, so one can imagine how biased these people can be when it comes to inter-ethnic violence. The events of March 1994 clearly demonstrated that the Serbs were at the hands of the terrorists without any protection provided to them whatsoever. And in 2004, March 2004, I would like to also specify that in Orahovac, the last of the 12 Serbs still living there - there were 10.000 before the war - died of hunger on the 15th of October, 2003 in the hospital of Kiskovgel [phoen]. He hadn't eaten for a month. His neighbours could not help him any more because they feared the violence at the hands of the KLA militia. This is the fate of the Serbs in Kosovo, and I fear that the situation will be the same as the one in Krajina where the international community will let the cleansing of the Serb population to take place without anybody reacting, and nobody will speak out. It will be the same situation in Krajina. In other words, the region will be totally cleansed of all Serbs.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Crepin. We are going to take a break now for 20 minutes. Mr. Milosevic?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I just have one more question, one more question, and then I will be over -- I will have finished with Blank page inserted to ensure the pagination between the English and French transcripts correspond Ms. Crepin.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So what were the reasons that you decided to come here to testify?

utterances.speaker: EVE CREPIN
utterances.text: I first of all wanted to testify how the Serb people have been unjustly treated and here their president has been unjustly treated also. I would like to testify and talk about the suffering of a number of people, and I hope I have done this adequately.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Crepin.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: We will now take a break for 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Madam Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: MS. DEL
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. Crepin, on my own behalf and also for the Judges' sake, I'd like to know precisely when, in which period, you were in Yugoslavia, and first and foremost whether you were in Yugoslavia always as a nurse. Let's start with March 1994. You stayed in Yugoslavia until June 1994, didn't you? You were in the military hospital in Glina.

utterances.speaker: EVE CREPIN
utterances.text: In the surgical service in Topusko.

utterances.speaker: MS. DEL
utterances.text: Yes. But if I understood you rightly, you first were in Sarajevo under -- within UNPROFOR.

utterances.speaker: EVE CREPIN
utterances.text: Yes, in February and March.

utterances.speaker: MS. DEL
utterances.text: First let me put on my headphones, because otherwise I can't hear you very well. So all in all, how many months did you spend?

utterances.speaker: EVE CREPIN
utterances.text: Four months for the two missions.

utterances.speaker: MS. DEL
utterances.text: Fine. So this was officially for the United Nations?

utterances.speaker: EVE CREPIN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. DEL
utterances.text: And then you went again and very often to Yugoslavia, but then on a private basis.

utterances.speaker: EVE CREPIN
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MS. DEL
utterances.text: Do you remember -- I'm merely interested in the periods because I have October 1994, then you returned to the Glina Hospital for a short stay. What is a short stay?

utterances.speaker: EVE CREPIN
utterances.text: I went back for about a fortnight every two or three months. I stayed either two or three weeks except for the Kosovo, where I stayed much longer, but otherwise I spent two or three weeks there each time.

utterances.speaker: MS. DEL
utterances.text: So that's always -- that was always in the Glina Hospital. And then you also made a visit to the Topusko hospital; is that right?

utterances.speaker: EVE CREPIN
utterances.text: No. That was as a military person. I was based in Topusko, I was working in the Glina Hospital, and when I returned on a private basis and no longer as a helmet to the Krajina area, I worked in the Glina Hospital.

utterances.speaker: MS. DEL
utterances.text: For two weeks?

utterances.speaker: EVE CREPIN
utterances.text: Two or three weeks each time.

utterances.speaker: MS. DEL
utterances.text: And you were working as a?

utterances.speaker: EVE CREPIN
utterances.text: Nurse.

utterances.speaker: MS. DEL
utterances.text: And what were you doing as a nurse? Because -- were you working in the anesthetics purposes?

utterances.speaker: EVE CREPIN
utterances.text: No, the operating theatre.

utterances.speaker: MS. DEL
utterances.text: I see. And that lasted until 1995?

utterances.speaker: EVE CREPIN
utterances.text: Until the fall of Krajina in 1995.

utterances.speaker: MS. DEL
utterances.text: In 1995, so you also became a citizen of the Krajina Republic?

utterances.speaker: EVE CREPIN
utterances.text: The Krajina people recognised and acknowledged my help and as thanks they gave me an identity card of the Krajina.

utterances.speaker: MS. DEL
utterances.text: Did you not -- you and Dr. Barriot did you not require citizenship as a token of your solidarity?

utterances.speaker: EVE CREPIN
utterances.text: No. It was really by way of thanks. People were so surprised that we were coming to help that they thought it was normal to welcome them in their fold as Krajina citizens.

utterances.speaker: MS. DEL
utterances.text: And you also spent some time for the French television.

utterances.speaker: EVE CREPIN
utterances.text: Several times.

utterances.speaker: MS. DEL
utterances.text: I see. Because I saw in the documents that we were given that you had received some authorisation for which channel?

utterances.speaker: EVE CREPIN
utterances.text: FR3.

utterances.speaker: MS. DEL
utterances.text: Not as a nurse, then.

utterances.speaker: EVE CREPIN
utterances.text: But yes, because there were several of us and I was going there to work, and once I was on this pass, I would go and see people, as I said earlier on, representatives who might help us work with the refugees. And by the same token, they allowed journalists to cover the situation. So the main objective was to work as a nurse or to go and see the refugees, and the second purpose was to go and see these people who very often gave interviews to journalists. And that made it possible for journalists to meet with these people.

utterances.speaker: MS. DEL
utterances.text: So they were Serb victims.

utterances.speaker: EVE CREPIN
utterances.text: Serb victims or leaders, as I said earlier on.

utterances.speaker: MS. DEL
utterances.text: So the French television was giving reports on the real situation, because before you said that Serbs were practically ignored, were not considered at all, but here you are telling us the opposite. You are telling us that the French television was accompanying you to film the victims, the refugees.

utterances.speaker: EVE CREPIN
utterances.text: Yes. But these recordings were not used, because the authorities, television authorities, would not broadcast them, so they stayed on the shelf.

utterances.speaker: MS. DEL
utterances.text: You said four or five times, then, because you said you went several times.

utterances.speaker: EVE CREPIN
utterances.text: No, I went several times. The documents were not broadcast. In the same way, I wrote a few articles for the press but there were hundreds of articles that were ignored. Only a few articles were published in the space of ten years whilst hundreds of them were not accepted.

utterances.speaker: MS. DEL
utterances.text: Regarding the victims, you mentioned the Serb victims. Did you have an opportunity to meet with victims from other ethnic groups, from Croat, Muslim victims? There were also victims among them.

utterances.speaker: EVE CREPIN
utterances.text: I never denied that there were victims in the three ethnic groups, because it was a civil war; therefore, per se, there were victims among all groups. I was very well positioned to see that so because I was in Sarajevo for several weeks and it's very unfortunate that all ethnic groups suffered from the war. I never said the contrary. I merely said that the Serbs, too, suffered. This is something nobody says.

utterances.speaker: MS. DEL
utterances.text: But if I heard you well this morning, you mainly mentioned Serb victims. I didn't hear you speak about Albanian victims, for instance, in Kosovo, because there were Albanian victims in Kosovo. There were victims everywhere.

utterances.speaker: EVE CREPIN
utterances.text: I mentioned Albanian wounded in the Pec hospital this morning.

utterances.speaker: MS. DEL
utterances.text: You were in Yugoslavia in 1994, and this goes until 1998.

utterances.speaker: MS. DEL
utterances.text: So 1999 even. And you read the indictment against Mr. Milosevic. Therefore, you know that regarding Croatia, mention is made of facts going back to 1991 and 1992. But at that time you were not in Croatia. You were not in Krajina, were you?

utterances.speaker: EVE CREPIN
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MS. DEL
utterances.text: So everything you say -- because, you know, you brought us back to the periods of 1991 and 1992, but that's only as a hearsay response.

utterances.speaker: EVE CREPIN
utterances.text: Yes. That's what the refugees experienced.

utterances.speaker: MS. DEL
utterances.text: But this is not what you yourself saw as a nurse.

utterances.speaker: EVE CREPIN
utterances.text: Yes. What I saw is the aggressive Croats, which is very right.

utterances.speaker: MS. DEL
utterances.text: That's what you say.

utterances.speaker: EVE CREPIN
utterances.text: No, I saw it myself. I spent months in Croatia, and I can tell you that I experienced this type of aggressiveness.

utterances.speaker: MS. DEL
utterances.text: You said that Milan Martic, the president, had said or written that any act of violence would be severely punished. In other words, there were acts of violence?

utterances.speaker: EVE CREPIN
utterances.text: Well, this is called prevention, pre-empting. He was trying to warn all police forces that if they were to commit any acts of violence, they would be punished. So that was by way of prevention. Blank page inserted to ensure the pagination between the English and French transcripts correspond

utterances.speaker: MS. DEL
utterances.text: But if it is a kind of prevention or pre-empting, that means that that happened, or was it just said like that?

utterances.speaker: EVE CREPIN
utterances.text: Just -- just to warn people. It was an interethnic conflict. Therefore, there was an aggressive behaviour by Croats which could have triggered, quite legitimately so, some reaction by the Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MS. DEL
utterances.text: You probably remember that in May 1995, President Milan Martic attacked Zagreb, that there were strikes on Zagreb.

utterances.speaker: EVE CREPIN
utterances.text: I remember Western Slavonia in 1995. Hundreds of people died.

utterances.speaker: MS. DEL
utterances.text: No, I mentioned Zagreb.

utterances.speaker: EVE CREPIN
utterances.text: Yes, but you don't understand Zagreb if you don't know what happened in 1995 in Western Slavonia. Croat forces relentlessly bombed civilian populations that were protected by the UN. There were hundreds of casualties, and President Milan Martic asked the international community to help. The community did not react, and therefore, in desperation, there was a reaction and the bombing of Zagreb was ordered, causing four or five casualties. So on the one hand you have unarmed civilians that were attacked in an UNPA, causing hundreds of casualties, and facing that you have a desperate reaction by a president calling the international community to the rescue and this call was left unanswered. Therefore, there is the bombing of Zagreb, causing four or five deaths.

utterances.speaker: MS. DEL
utterances.text: Very well. From June 1994 to August 1995, you were, as you said, again in the Glina Hospital. Were you there on a regular basis? Does that mean that you were there all the time or only for the two or three weeks you mentioned?

utterances.speaker: EVE CREPIN
utterances.text: It was regular, because I went there regularly every two or there months for two or three weeks.

utterances.speaker: MS. DEL
utterances.text: Now that's clear, because otherwise I had failed to understand. The Flash and Storm operations, you were not there as an UNPROFOR member but privately.

utterances.speaker: EVE CREPIN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. DEL
utterances.text: Where were you?

utterances.speaker: EVE CREPIN
utterances.text: In Bosnia, in Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: MS. DEL
utterances.text: You spoke about the Serb population. Do you remember what happened to the other minorities that were still in Banja Luka? There were still Croats and Muslims there. What happened to them?

utterances.speaker: EVE CREPIN
utterances.text: I mainly saw the refugees leaving Western Slavonia for the Flash operation and Krajina for the Storm operation. So I looked after the Serb refugees that had to leave in a hurry.

utterances.speaker: MS. DEL
utterances.text: But in Banja Luka there were also Croats and Muslims that had to flee.

utterances.speaker: EVE CREPIN
utterances.text: In Western Slavonia.

utterances.speaker: MS. DEL
utterances.text: You were in Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: EVE CREPIN
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. DEL
utterances.text: They had to leave Banja Luka because the Serbs were coming.

utterances.speaker: EVE CREPIN
utterances.text: As I said throughout my testimony this morning, the two communities, the Croats and the Muslims, were supported and helped by NGOs. I looked after people who were totally left abandoned, nobody cared about.

utterances.speaker: MS. DEL
utterances.text: You said that nobody looked after them.

utterances.speaker: EVE CREPIN
utterances.text: Yes. That's unfortunately so. I took care of them, and I did my best to help people that nobody helped. There's no point in having ten NGOs look after one group whilst there is one group left totally alone. It's better to spread the help and support so everybody can be helped and aided fairly.

utterances.speaker: MS. DEL
utterances.text: In August 1995, you said that you met with Mladic, Karadzic, Plavsic, Krajisnik.

utterances.speaker: EVE CREPIN
utterances.text: Starting from the fall of the Krajina area.

utterances.speaker: MS. DEL
utterances.text: Regarding Karadzic, did you maintain contact with him?

utterances.speaker: EVE CREPIN
utterances.text: No, I didn't.

utterances.speaker: MS. DEL
utterances.text: Especially not now, I suppose.

utterances.speaker: EVE CREPIN
utterances.text: No, that's not connected with that. I never had an opportunity to meet with him again.

utterances.speaker: MS. DEL
utterances.text: Did you meet Mladic?

utterances.speaker: EVE CREPIN
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MS. DEL
utterances.text: Because one of the books you wrote together with Dr. Barriot, which is A People is Being Murdered --

utterances.speaker: EVE CREPIN
utterances.text: Yes, the people of Krajina.

utterances.speaker: MS. DEL
utterances.text: You left some space for Karadzic, who wrote a chapter, for Mladic, who wrote a chapter of the book, for Martic who did the introduction, and we were lucky enough to read it all, but in this book you wrote nothing says anything as to your sources. Where do you get those -- this information from, because it is a book, a comment on history, but there's no footnote stating your sources.

utterances.speaker: EVE CREPIN
utterances.text: This is a bibliography towards the end of the book.

utterances.speaker: MS. DEL
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: EVE CREPIN
utterances.text: Mentioning the sources.

utterances.speaker: MS. DEL
utterances.text: But there is no real mention, and I'm not going into details here.

utterances.speaker: EVE CREPIN
utterances.text: But if you have the bibliography, you can see all the books we quote.

utterances.speaker: MS. DEL
utterances.text: Yes. But precisely there are some points where I can't agree with you. But I'm not going to delve into this. In the course of your meetings with Mladic, with Karadzic, and other people, this is now August 1995, did you mention Srebrenica? Did you mention what happened in Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: EVE CREPIN
utterances.text: We talked a lot about the refugees, and together with Patrick Barriot, they talked indeed about Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MS. DEL
utterances.text: Because I was somewhat amazed to note that there is no mention whatsoever of Srebrenica whilst that, Srebrenica, is one of the most serious, most egregious acts. Did you mention this with Mladic?

utterances.speaker: EVE CREPIN
utterances.text: Yes, we talked a little about it.

utterances.speaker: MS. DEL
utterances.text: A little? 8.000 Muslims?

utterances.speaker: EVE CREPIN
utterances.text: There is no evidence of that and so far investigators, in ten years' time, in their reports mention 2.500 bodies that were exhumed. So there's no evidence so far so I can't tell you anything about something that has not been tried yet.

utterances.speaker: MS. DEL
utterances.text: I didn't want to really discuss Srebrenica with you. I just wanted to know from you whether you spoke about Srebrenica with the people you met, with Karadzic and Mladic. Do you think that they are heroes?

utterances.speaker: EVE CREPIN
utterances.text: You mean heroes?

utterances.speaker: MS. DEL
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: EVE CREPIN
utterances.text: I think that they're people who looked after their people and made sure that that population could stay alive in the face of an aggressor who was doing everything to eradicate them and in the face of an international community that was trying its level best to worsen the conflict prevailing in the former Yugoslavia. I think that these people looked after their population. They did their best to protect their people.

utterances.speaker: MS. DEL
utterances.text: And do you know that we hold them as criminals and that they're being indicted?

utterances.speaker: EVE CREPIN
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. DEL
utterances.text: Do you also know that in the Flash and Storm operations other people were indicted who were non-Serbs?

utterances.speaker: EVE CREPIN
utterances.text: Well, Tudjman died without being indicted.

utterances.speaker: MS. DEL
utterances.text: I don't want to give names here.

utterances.speaker: EVE CREPIN
