utterances.text: I know that all the people who are responsible were not indicted. Tomislav Mercep was even elected in Eastern Slavonia, I believe.

utterances.speaker: MS. DEL
utterances.text: I prefer not to mention names. I'm just telling you right now that people who are responsible for the Flash and Storm operations were indicted. Now, let's talk about Kosovo. How long you were in Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: EVE CREPIN
utterances.text: I spent June 1998.

utterances.speaker: MS. DEL
utterances.text: In Pristina.

utterances.speaker: EVE CREPIN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. DEL
utterances.text: As a nurse?

utterances.speaker: EVE CREPIN
utterances.text: Yes. Blank page inserted to ensure the pagination between the English and French transcripts correspond

utterances.speaker: MS. DEL
utterances.text: Where did you work as a nurse?

utterances.speaker: EVE CREPIN
utterances.text: I'm a nurse and I was a member of the steering group for the Krajina Serbs. I paid a first visit in the hope that I will be able to go to Pec as a nurse, and as I explained this morning, I -- it was not possible because the dean, Popovic, said I shouldn't go because the KLA fighting and the blocking of roads. So I couldn't go to Pec as a nurse. And then I was in Pec in July and August 1998, where I worked as a nurse.

utterances.speaker: MS. DEL
utterances.text: So if you worked as a nurse, you were working in a hospital?

utterances.speaker: EVE CREPIN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. DEL
utterances.text: In which hospital?

utterances.speaker: EVE CREPIN
utterances.text: In the Pec hospital.

utterances.speaker: MS. DEL
utterances.text: There's only one?

utterances.speaker: EVE CREPIN
utterances.text: I don't know. Well, I was in Pec, but I don't know how many hospitals there are.

utterances.speaker: MS. DEL
utterances.text: Yes, in the Pec hospital. You speak about the exodus of Serbs. Were you able to see that there was an exodus of other ethnic groups or communities from Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: EVE CREPIN
utterances.text: I was in Serbia during the bombing campaign, but during the bombing campaign, the Albanians fled from Kosovo, as did the Roma, the Gypsies, the Serbs. The NATO bombing caused the exodus of all groups in the population, sparing nobody. And among the casualties you can find Albanians, Serbs. There are convoys or columns of Albanians who were bombed because they sought refuge. There were a hundred thousand Albanians who were taken in by Serbia. And Serbia is the only multi-ethnic country to have welcomed Albanians. Unfortunately, Albanian convoys were targeted as were Serb convoys.

utterances.speaker: MS. DEL
utterances.text: So there was no discrimination?

utterances.speaker: EVE CREPIN
utterances.text: Yes, there was no discrimination by the NATO bombing. There is no difference when you bomb from 5.000 metres high up in the sky.

utterances.speaker: MS. DEL
utterances.text: I'd like to ask you this: Did you also go to camps, to refugee camps where there were not only Serbs, because there were refugee camps of other ethnic groups? What I'm trying to hear from you is whether you were truly independent or whether you were only concerned about the situation where Serbs were regarded as victims.

utterances.speaker: EVE CREPIN
utterances.text: Forty thousand Muslims were taken in the Krajina.

utterances.speaker: MS. DEL
utterances.text: You went to visit them?

utterances.speaker: EVE CREPIN
utterances.text: Yes. Well, I risked my life, madam, for the Muslims in Sarajevo. I helped an armoured convoy of the population. There were Serbs and Muslims all together. So I risked my life for those people.

utterances.speaker: MS. DEL
utterances.text: Did you go to camps where there were Croats?

utterances.speaker: EVE CREPIN
utterances.text: No, I didn't, but I risked my life during those missions for Serbs and Muslims alike. I was in the field.

utterances.speaker: MS. DEL
utterances.text: Nobody doubts that.

utterances.speaker: EVE CREPIN
utterances.text: Yes, but I wanted to say it. I experienced it, and I took risks, and I did not mind my own life in order to save other people or to help them, whether they be Muslims or Croats.

utterances.speaker: MS. DEL
utterances.text: Well, that's what I wanted to know from you. I wanted to know whether you were only focused on the Serb victims. There are or there were victims in all camps.

utterances.speaker: EVE CREPIN
utterances.text: I'm a humanitarian person before all, and there's no politics in that. MS. DEL PONTE: [Interpretation] Mr. President, Your Honours , this is an exhibit in the file of this case. I just want to mention in page 6 -- it is Exhibit 145. I just want to quote one single sentence. I could quote several --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Madam Prosecutor, what is the document? MS. DEL PONTE: It's the report, OSCE. The report OSCE, Exhibit 145.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Under Orders. Yes, proceed. MS. DEL PONTE: Page 6. Page 6.

utterances.speaker: MS. DEL
utterances.text: I quote: "Deliberate and unlawful killings of civilians, extrajudicial executions were a key part of the cleansing campaign. Throughout the province civilians who were clearly non-combatants, including women and some children, were murdered by Serbian police, Yugoslav army soldiers, and associated paramilitary forces in execution-style killings." [Interpretation] I just quoted this one sentence to challenge what you just said regarding the OSCE report. Of course, you said something, and I quote the report, so this is the reason why I'm telling you that the OSCE report is very different from the conclusion you draw from the report.

utterances.speaker: EVE CREPIN
utterances.text: This sentence doesn't specify when the acts were committed.

utterances.speaker: MS. DEL
utterances.text: Quite --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Madam Prosecutor, is that an OSCE report or the Human Rights Watch "Under Orders"? Is it not written by Human Rights Watch? MS. DEL PONTE: I hope it is the -- no, it's Human Rights Watch. I'm sorry. OSCE. I have in my hands the OSCE report, but it was the Human Rights Watch report, I'm sorry. It had been passed on to me as though it was the OSCE report. I'm sorry. I have another report, and this time I hope it is the OSCE report. It is, yes. [In English] October 1999. [Interpretation] But of course I did not have time to look into it.

utterances.speaker: MS. DEL
utterances.text: I have another question for you, Ms. Crepin. You were in touch with authorities. Who did you have contact with? Which were the national authorities you were in contact with?

utterances.speaker: EVE CREPIN
utterances.text: Milan Martic, the president of Krajina; Mr. Karadzic; General Ratko Mladic.

utterances.speaker: MS. DEL
utterances.text: Yes, you said so. But under which -- what circumstances?

utterances.speaker: EVE CREPIN
utterances.text: When we made trips trying to find refugees to see how they were looked after, whether they were looked after or not, what they needed. And we were also during Vidovdan Day in 1995 together with Karadzic and Mladic because we happened to be there and we were invited. You know, there were so few people helping the Serbs, and the former Yugoslavia being a very small country, it was a matter of fact that we were invited to certain events.

utterances.speaker: MS. DEL
utterances.text: Well, you spoke about -- you spoke about politics, of course.

utterances.speaker: EVE CREPIN
utterances.text: Yes, about politics, about the situation of refugees, about the fact that France has abandoned the Serbs. We mentioned all that. There was also the regret that French would no longer help the suffering Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MS. DEL
utterances.text: Yes, we mentioned all that. So your experience is one, as you stated earlier on, that prompted you to ask to be a witness in the Milosevic case?

utterances.speaker: EVE CREPIN
utterances.text: Yes. My testimony was very important to me, because I wanted at long last to voice the suffering by the Serbs. And I promised all these people to testify to their suffering, and this was an opportunity for me to say what happened really on the ground.

utterances.speaker: MS. DEL
utterances.text: Very well. So you want to testify to the suffering by the Serbs.

utterances.speaker: EVE CREPIN
utterances.text: Yes, absolutely.

utterances.speaker: MS. DEL
utterances.text: But you are not in a position to testify as to the guilt or innocence of Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: EVE CREPIN
utterances.text: I'm testifying to say what I really saw on the ground in Krajina, in Kosovo, about the NATO bombing campaign, about what I was able to see.

utterances.speaker: MS. DEL
utterances.text: I have another OSCE report, Exhibit 106. MS. DEL PONTE: And it is again page 6, Mr. President. There is one paragraph of page 6 dealing with, but I didn't have time to read it,

utterances.speaker: MS. DEL
utterances.text: They reacted to the KLA attacks, and they arrested people. I'm not going to read this out. I just wanted to quote this paragraph to be found in page 6 - it is the second paragraph of this OSCE report - just to mention the fact that this is different from the conclusions drawn by the witness. I have no further questions. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Prosecutor. Any re-examination, Mr. Milosevic?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Ms. Crepin, just one simple question. Prior to 1993, had you been to Serbia? Blank page inserted to ensure the pagination between the English and French transcripts correspond

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Never.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Ms. Crepin, that concludes your evidence, and you may leave.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, we have considered your submission about the next witness. We're of the view that we'll have to hear the evidence. If during the course of the witness's testimony anything arises that you wish to comment on, then of course you may do so. Mr. Milosevic, your next witness.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Patrick Barriot.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I understand the next witness was scheduled to be here at 11.45, so we're running ahead of time. So we'll take the break now for 20 minutes and then return.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Let the witness make the declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Please sit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mr. Barriot.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Just briefly, could you tell us something about your professional career, your CV.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BARRIOT
utterances.text: Good day to you, Mr. President. My name is Patrick Barriot, I'm a colonel in the French army. That's my rank. I'm a doctor, and I'm a specialist in emergency services and emergency toxicological diseases. I've been working for 25 years in the French army and I'm also an anaesthetist. I have been working for the French Fire Brigade, the 11th Paratrooper Division, civil intervention unit, and a surgical mobile unit in the former Yugoslavia. When I left the army, I was the head doctor of the civil security unit and in charge of intervention operations and advisor to the prefect and in charge of Civil Defence, and I was working for the minister of defence and I held the rank of colonel. When I left the army in 1998, I was appointed expert on hospital matters, and I'm also a lecturer in a number of medical facilities, institutes and a number of schools in France or universities. I'm part of a number of association of scientists. I've written ten or so books on emergency medical care, and I have written a hundred or so articles that have been published in international reviews and the international journal of medicine. I'm also an expert on any matters relating to non-conventional armament systems and terrorism. I therefore have speciality in civil security and civil protection area. As I told you, I was the head doctor of the civil security in the French armed forces. I also attended the training course of the UNHCR to become an expert on emergency situation in Lausanne, and I was also in charge at that time of the coordination of Aid Relief, a non-governmental organisation. In the emergency units I'm also an expert on unconventional arms. I have been involved in a number of military conflicts in the Middle East, in Africa, in a number of countries in the world. I've just written a book on massive destruction arms with a preface by Pierre-Marie Gallois, who is the leader in the nuclear deterrence programme. In 1986 I took part in the RER protection, the terrorist attack, in 1995 in particular, the attack on the B Line of the Paris underground, the Saint Michel underground station. I was part of an expert group of civil security group in France that went to Tokyo at the time of the attack on -- the gas attack in the underground in Tokyo, and I'm also a member of a number of research groups working on risk assessment and terrorist risk assessment. More specifically, bioterrorist programme and response provided, which is funded by a strategic research group Centre Biotops. I would like to finish off by saying that I've never been indicted nor suspected of anything. I am -- have the title of Order of the Merit, and I have received four medals from the prefect of the French police and three letters from the Ministry of Defence of the armed forces and Ministry of Cooperation for operations undertaken abroad with a view to protecting the civilian population.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: For what did you receive the title of Order of Merit, and from whom?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I received the national Order of Merit, assigned by President Francois Mitterand for those actions undertaken abroad in Albania, in Kurdistan, the Iraqi part of Kurdistan and other regions in the world. I'm 49, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: And you had your medical degree before you went into the army?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes -- no. I became a doctor when I joined the army. I joined the army when I was 18, so I conducted my medical studies whilst I was in the army.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Milosevic, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Dr. Barriot, tell us briefly what experience you have with respect to the conflicts on the territory of the former Yugoslavia or, rather, where were you in the former Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BARRIOT
utterances.text: Yes. I shall briefly underline this in three parts. So as far as Croatia is concerned, I was a Blue Helmet in the former Yugoslavia, in Krajina more specifically, in Topusko, close to Glina, in the southern sector of UNPROFOR for a number of months. I moved around to -- I went to Banja Luka, Northern Dalmatia, and also I moved around the rest of Croatia. I went to Zagreb, and I went to the Bihac pocket, Velika Kladusa, more specifically, because that was very close to Glina and Topusko. I then, in the years 1994, 1995, went back to Krajina, working there for two humanitarian aid organisations, more specifically Humanitaire Krajina, which was created by Bucan, and Teleobjectif, the humanitarian aid organisation which was created by Marica Mathei. And I was present in the region at the time of the Storm and Flash operations launched by the Croat forces. I was, in 1995, appointed by Milan Martic official representative of the Serb Republic of Krajina in Paris. I wrote a book entitled The Murder of a People, the Serbs in Krajina. This book was prefaced by the President Milan Martic, who also wrote an entire chapter on the history of Krajina. In addition, I went on assignments with the French television crew FR3, Christian de Garnet [phoen], Mourad Tabouche, who wanted to conduct interviews of Milan Martic. So I enabled them to organise these interviews. In addition, I wrote ten or so articles on the history of Krajina. So much for Croatia. As far as Bosnia is concerned, I went many times to Bosnia in 1994 and 1995. On the one hand as a representative of the Serb Republic of Krajina, I was in charge of assessing the needs of the refugees there. I met Radovan Karadzic several times. I also met other key personalities like Ratko Mladic whom I met on several occasions in 1995. I wrote a number of testimonies during those years at the -- The Devils Are Let Loose, which is published at L'Age d'Homme and another testimony on Serbia which was also published by the publishing house L'Age d'Homme, A Murder of a Nation, a Murder of a People, the Serbs in Krajina. I published a paper by Radovan Karadzic and a paper by General Ratko Mladic. Blank page inserted to ensure the pagination between the English and French transcripts correspond So I enabled a television crew, FR3, a French television channel, to conduct interviews of Radovan Karadzic and General Ratko Mladic, particularly an interview which took place in September of 1995 and which was broadcast in France at the beginning of October 1995. Now, as far as the third part is concerned, Kosovo and Serbia, I was in Kosovo in 1998, in the summer of 1998, where I visited Kosovo and I moved around from the north to the south of the Kosovo. I also went to Serbia. I went to Belgrade, in the Belgrade area, and during the NATO strikes, March and April of 1999. So I was in the former Yugoslavia, in Croatia, in Bosnia, in Kosovo, and in Serbia at crucial times, at moments -- at a moment when these very important events were unfolding and -- between that time until 1999.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: What were your motives for coming here to testify today?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BARRIOT
utterances.text: Well, my motivation is largely due to this large gap I noticed between what was happening on the ground. I was a member of the military, I was a member of humanitarian aid organisation, I was a representative of the Serb government in Krajina. And I realised that there was this huge gap between what was happening on the ground and what the media was broadcasting or talking about, and the press, the print press. So I would like to testify about this. I felt that greater injustice had been done to the Serb people, and I wanted to testify about what the Serb experienced during this war. This suffering has been overlooked entirely and I have come to testify in the name of the Serb people because I feel that it is the Serb people, and I say it with a great deal of emotion, I would like to talk about what I have seen, what I have heard throughout this period of time. I would like to say that I do not belong to any political party, whether it be in France or abroad. I would like to make this clear, because very often members of the military who have sided with the Serbs have been accused of belonging to extremist groups. Rene Bachelet, in December 1995, took pity on the Serbs in Sarajevo, in the Tivica areas, Kravica and Vogosca, and he said that he had to choose between luggage and a coffin, and he was accused of having sided with Serb extremists. I'd like to say that overall the French extreme right is much closer to the Croats than it is to the Serbs. And Ante Gotovina has many more friends --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: You've answered the question about your motivation. Next question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Barriot, while you were in the Balkans, were you always accompanied by Ms. Crepin?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In most cases, yes, we were together. I can't say that we were always together, but we were more often than not together.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: And if you could tell me what a representative of the Serbian Krajina is. I heard the same thing from Ms. Crepin as well. So both of you are representatives of that entity, and what were you doing in that capacity in France?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, in my capacity as representative of the Serbian Krajina, I undertook a number of things. I tried to get the attention of the media. This was one of our primary objectives. This is the objective outlined by President Milan Martic. It was important that the media understand what the situation actually was on the ground and the Serbs in Krajina and Croatia were suffering. And this had been -- as this had been totally overlooked by the media. So to begin with it was a matter of clearly explaining the situation on the ground and to make sure that a clear picture was provided because it was not in the press at the time. The second objective was of a humanitarian nature. We had to coordinate aid relief, because nobody was interested in the Serbs of Krajina. Nobody came to help them. They were -- had been provided with no outside help. It was for us to assess their needs and, if possible, provide some aid relief, some basic commodities and some medication and medical supplies.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Who appointed you a representative of the Krajina?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] President Milan Martic. And I think I indicated in the documents the official letter signed by President Milan Martic. These are part of the documents I provided to the Tribunal which I can give you if you so wish.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Where is that in the documents, Mr. Milosevic, the letter of appointment?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm trying to find it. Yes, here it is. It's tab 4. Tab 4. Decision signed by President Milan Martic, "[In English] Opening of representative office of the Republic of Serbian Krajina in Paris."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: At that time you were still a member of the -- you had a post in the army at that time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I did. I was a senior officer in the French army, and I was nevertheless appointed by President Martic to represent the Serbian Republic of Krajina. This was indicated in an Agence France Presse dispatch. Mate Granic, as a result of it, was extremely angry. He was the Croat minister of foreign affairs, and he -- he filed a complaint officially. I was insulted in the Vjesnik newspaper that called me a fascist for having been appointed a representative. They stated in any case that the Serbian Republic of Krajina did not exist. But as far as I'm concerned, it did exist and does still exist.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: No question arose of a possible conflict between your being in the French army and being a representative of the Krajina?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, a conflict arose at that time. The -- my commanders asked me to refuse this. They said that I had been manipulated by the Serb authorities, but this was not the case at all. So I refused to take that back, and I refused to sign that document, because I was doing it knowing full well what I was doing. And that is why I left the army shortly afterwards. But if I had accepted to take that back, I would have still held my rank, but I did not want to do this because I wanted to be honoured by this nomination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Did you describe all the difficulties that you encountered when stating your views about the situation in Yugoslavia? Did you have any other complications or difficulties?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BARRIOT
utterances.text: Yes. I would like to emphasise that -- the fact that all other people who wanted to interpret this conflict different ways or express what they had seen on the ground was in contradiction with what the media was saying and stating at the time. Admittedly, the military were in the forefront and have applied these repressive measures over other issues that came up, of course. Our telephones were tapped and I received a number of death threats. But I was not the only person to be in that situation, because all the military who tried to understand what was actually happening on the ground, and whenever they tried to establish a closer contacts with the Serbs -- Sir Michael Rose, for instance, his telephone conversations were also tapped because there was -- all the contacts he tried to establish with the Serbs had been obstructed. I also mentioned the case of Jean-Rene Bachelet, who was insulted for having defended the Serbs in certain areas of Sarajevo in 1995. So in general terms, all the French military or military of other countries who tried to explain what they actually saw on the ground were asked to hold their tongues, and sometimes in a rather violent manner. But this applied not only to the military but also applied to diplomats. When the Storm operation was launched and Mr. Carl Bildt said the Knin massacre was extremely -- extremely serious offence that could lead to the indictment of Tudjman, Zagreb and Washington told him to hold his tongue. When criticism was levelled at UNMIK, Mr. Kouchner, what he was doing with Kosovo, he was told to be quiet. Mr. Bisbier [phoen] told him Blank page inserted to ensure the pagination between the English and French transcripts correspond to shut up, which was a rather language used by rogues. Nevertheless, every time somebody tried to provide a different view of the situation, a view which was objective and which was in line with what was happening on the ground, were told to hold their tongues. The case of Mr. Regis Debre, for instance, a French intellectual who was called a revisionist, or a journalist like Jacques Merlinot who lost his job, just about, for having talked about what he saw. So I'd like to stress this, and I'm very happy to be able to express myself freely on this count because this is something quite unusual, and we have always been asked to hold our tongues when we wanted to speak out the truth and describe what was actually happening on the ground.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, you can express yourself freely, but relevantly. Yes, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I hope, Mr. Robinson, that what the witness said a moment ago is quite relevant, I would say.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Barriot, in view of the fact that we see that you were a high-ranking officer of the French army, frequently abroad on missions, I would like to ask you the following question: Did you have any links with the French intelligence services?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BARRIOT
utterances.text: Yes. I was in close contact with the French intelligence services largely due to the fact that the job I had in 1994, I was the head doctor of civil security and moving about all the time abroad in very sensitive areas. I was in touch with the DGSE agents, the external security units which are the equivalent of the Military Intelligence Services in France. As of 1995 onwards, I was also in touch with DST agents, Direction de la Surete du Territoire, which is the equivalent of civil intelligence services in France. And I would like to specify how this happened. At the end of 1995, as I was in Pale, in the presence of Mr. Mourad Ay Tabouche, who was the TV French reporter, I was accosted by Mr. Jugoslav Petrusic, also known under the nickname of Dominik. Mr. Jugoslav Petrusic came up to me and quite clearly knew me well, or at least knew a lot about my personal life and my professional life, and he told me he was working with the French DST, the Direction de la Surete du Territoire, and gave me the names -- gave me the name and number of his employer, in other words, his boss at the DST. He also stated that there had been plans to do away with me and that a contract had been signed to that effect, and to liquidate me. So at that time, the French reporter was present, and he can confirm this -- this is important, because it's the first time that Mr. Rene Tabouche met with Jugoslav Petrusic. I mention this because it is important for the following events. Mr. Tabouche conducted reports in Bosnia thanks to Mr. Jugoslav Petrusic, with the help of this gentleman.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, please, do you know anything about the freeing of the French pilots in 1995?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BARRIOT
utterances.text: Yes. This is a sensitive issue and an important one. And Mr. Jugoslav Petrusic played an important part in this release. I'd like to say that Tabouche made a report on the liberation of the French pilots in 1995, and it so happens that this report was censored by the French authorities because in this report you see that an important sum of money which was to be used as a ransom - I would like to state that the Serb authorities had not ransomed anybody - but they stated in this report that the large sum of money had been embezzled by French politicians on this occasion. Let me explain. Pilots were held by the Serbs in Bosnia. They were held prisoner. The French DST, in November of 1995, sent two negotiating teams to ensure the release of these two pilots. What I am about to say is very important. The first negotiating group was headed by Raymond Martre [phoen] and Pierre-Marie Gallois was to head this negotiating team. Pierre-Marie Gallois went to Bosnia where he met General Ratko Mladic on the 17th of November, 1995. When he came back to Paris, General Pierre-Marie Gallois described his mission and said that General Mladic had not asked for any ransom. All he wanted was a handshake with the Chief of Staff, General Dwynne [phoen] of the French armed forces in exchange of the release of the prisoners. Strangely enough, a second negotiating team was sent there a few days later. Jean-Charles Marchiani was academie de marquois [phoen] in charge of this. They -- these two people met General Mladic on the 25th of November, 1995; i.e., eight days after the first meeting with Pierre-Marie Gallois, and back in France they said that General Mladic doesn't mind freeing the pilots but in exchange of a ransom of a couple of thousand euros. So at the end of the day, our French pilots were released on the 12th of December, 1995, after General Mladic had shook hands with the Chief of Staff of the French air force. But I would like to state that General Mladic did not receive a single cent and --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I'm sorry to interrupt. I perhaps ought to have interrupted earlier. I know that this evidence is likely to feature within the case, and it may be from the accused's list of witnesses there is another witness who has direct evidence on it, but it's not clear to me, it may be my mistake, whether this witness is relating his own personal knowledge or if he's relating an account from someone else. And it may be helpful to the Chamber before we move any further on this topic to find out what his source of knowledge of all this is, because I'm not entirely clear myself.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Did you lead evidence about this?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: There's evidence before you about the French pilots, and their history is not unimportant. It's not particularly important, but it's not totally unimportant. You will recall it was first mentioned, I think, by Lilic, but -- perhaps not first by certainly mentioned by him. The way it integrates in the case as a whole is somewhat complicated and I certainly don't want to go into it now, but it would be helpful to know whether this is first, second, or third-hand evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Barriot. Mr. Barriot -- are you hearing me? Mr. Barriot, I'm asking you, the information that you have given, how did you get it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, the information I've just conveyed was given to me directly by various sources, be they French intelligence services or Pierre-Marie Gallois, or Mr. Jugoslav Petrusic whom I met personally on several occasions, or yet Mr. Mourad Ay Tabouche. So I didn't quite understand the reservations expressed by Mr. Nice. I think this is a very important problem, because I think it shows once again the way information is manipulated and the way in which the honour of General Mladic was tarnished by saying that he asked for a ransom whilst he never asked anything of the kind. And I want to stress once again that the report by Mr. Tabouche was censored by the French authorities, not without reason. So I think that we are in the very heart of the matter, and this is a major problem.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Did you remain in touch with Jugoslav Petrusic?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BARRIOT
utterances.text: I met Mr. Petrusic some months ago. He lives in Paris, and he told me that he had been interviewed at length by ICTY people. So I met him. He came to see me following a public meeting in which we spoke about Serbia. He came up to me and again he talked for a long time on this report regarding the release of the French pilots which he had done with Mr. Tabouche. He gave me his mobile number and his other telephone number, asking him -- asking me to call him again, which I did not do. I did not get in touch with him since.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Let's move on. I'll try to deal very efficiently with a host of issues. You said yourself that you headed the medical sector of civilian security and you are now a member of this government expert group that is charged with trying to see whether there would be any terrorist attacks launched against France. So I imagine this is a subject that is close to you.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BARRIOT
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Now, bearing that in mind, owing to the fact that you spent a long time in the territory of the former Yugoslavia, you learned a lot about what happened there. Do you know anything about the presence and activity of any terrorist groups in Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BARRIOT
utterances.text: Yes, of course. As early as in 1994, the Western intelligence services, even though they underestimated the threat, were perfectly aware that there were in Bosnia terrorist groups connected to the GIA from Algeria and also connected with al Qaeda.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honours, can I again respectfully suggest that before we allow this evidence in, even subject to whether it's relevant, we establish what his source of knowledge is. The Chamber will recall that with witnesses who have sought to rely on intelligence material that they were not then in a position or willing to disclose, the evidence was sometimes blocked before it was given or indicated as evidence that couldn't be accepted. Now, I'm not sure if this witness is speaking --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Or of very little value.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Or of very little value. I'm not sure whether this witness is speaking from his own knowledge or whether he's speaking of rumour or whether he's going to say that he had direct access to some intelligence, and if so, if he's going to identify the intelligence and enable us to see it, but at the moment it's very hard to get a grip on what it is we're being told about.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Barriot, can you help us with the reference that you've made to "Western intelligence services"? What specific source did you have for this information?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I -- I want to say this once again. I said that in the beginning when I introduced myself precisely in order not to have to repeat it all the time, and I say this again to Mr. Nice: The knowledge I have of the problems is not something that I learned from newspapers. I take this from my work, from what I did. I was the head doctor for civilian security, and this position is connected to the Ministry of the Interior. And when you have such a position, you have a connection with the prefect of civilian security and, therefore, also with the minister of the interior. When I was dispatched abroad, for instance, to Tokyo as a specialist regarding terrorism, I say it once again and I'm sorry I have to repeat this, I had to work during the numerous terrorist attacks there were in France and in Paris. I am part of many research groups on the matter, and I think that I have proved that I have contacts at the highest level in intelligence services. So you should maybe wait until you've heard me out before you doubt my credentials.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Barriot, what is the specific source for this information?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I have to repeat this: I spent entire years within emergency units in specialised units in the fight against terrorism, and I have gathered all the information I now have in course of those activities. I can't give you a signed paper, papers signed by the director of intelligence services in order to prove what I say.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: This is just information, then, that you have picked up generally through the discharge of your functions?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Exactly so. During the start of my activities as an individual, as a senior officer in charge of public security in France.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, it would seem to me that this is unlikely to be of any value. We're not going to be able to see documents, it would appear. We're not going to be able to cross-examine to the documents and the witness doesn't appear to be saying that this is material that he received firsthand. Beyond that, the material may in any event be irrelevant. So I would invite the Chamber to require the accused to move on to another topic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, let me hear from you on this point before ruling.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Robinson, we have established that Colonel Barriot headed the medical sector of the civilian security of France, and that he is still even now a member of a government group in charge of forecasting possible terrorist attacks against France. So he is in a position to have access to the kind of information that we're talking about. The only question Mr. Nice can put is whether this witness is telling the truth or lying. As for all the documents we have here, they can only confirm that everything the witness has been saying is true, that this is an honourable man, that this is a man who is completely honest on the one hand, and on the other hand that he has access to information that he did not obtain by reading the newspapers or hearing rumours, as was put here, but he was a former senior military officer and now a member of a governmental group. And I imagine that if somebody is head of the civilian sector, I imagine he gets information in order to be able to carry out the job he has been entrusted with.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: And what would be the relevance of the evidence?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The relevance is in the fact that it is indubitably correct that certain governments in the West supported terrorism in Bosnia-Herzegovina which produced fatal consequences. When the previous witness testified, you were wondering whether this was a crime above all crimes or whether it was a kind of tit for tat. There is no way of -- this is no way to deal with this. This was a conflict that was tragic for all sides, but within a context we have to view the causes and the consequences of everything that happened in the territory of the former Yugoslavia. I think that this picture is going to become increasingly clear to you as the proceedings go on. I'm not referring only to this witness but also other witnesses so that we can see things in their true light, not in this distorted light, as has been the case so far.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Your Honours, if I could add a point to this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: The witness is entitled to speak to his own knowledge. He can cite the support of sources for that knowledge, which may be documentary or may be from his own experience because of the role which he carried. The witness may be cross-examined as to the validity of that source of his knowledge, and indeed it may be a matter of weight at the end of the day as to how supportive and how the Trial Chamber is convinced about the validity of the testimony of the witness on various issues contained within it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Any observation on relevance?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: There seem to be issues within this trial that the accused is genuinely advancing in contradiction of the case against him by the Prosecutor. We know that his case against the Prosecutor is that this is a manufactured trial against him, that there are sources who were involved in this Prosecution who have been against him and his country for a period of time, who have been acting for his downfall. Therefore, if such sources, if such influences, if you like, are revealed to have had power within events and matters in relation to this prosecution, it may well be then that the accused is able to establish one of the tenets of his defence in relation to aspects of the case against him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: If that's correct, Mr. Kay, then it's all the more important that the evidence is given in a way which would enable the Trial Chamber to assign some weight to it. And the way I understand the witness's response so far, it is to say, "You guys up there don't need to bother about the source of my knowledge. I'm an honourable man, I've got a wide range of experience, it's the year 2005 now, and therefore I've accumulated even more and therefore I'm even more reliable," when we're dealing with what he says specifically is the knowledge by Western intelligence services at a particular time in the fairly distant past. So it seems to me he ought to be able to give us an indication, even in fairly broad -- he hasn't even given it in fairly broad terms of the source of that particular piece of information. That's my difficulty.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: I understand that entirely, and in many respects parties run the risk of losing their points if they don't put the best evidence forward and evidence that they might reasonably anticipate a Tribunal, the triers of fact, to want to hear. It doesn't diminish from the point that's being made. But the weight, which is a word Your Lordships -- Your Honours have used in relation to this issue, is another matter, and that's something that the litigant in person must bear in mind in trying to convince on a particular point. I hope those are helpful observations.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: It's weight, not admissibility.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: We may not be able to attach much weight at all to the evidence if we don't have a source revealed and if the Prosecutor, in particular, is not able to cross-examine on it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: I'm sure that's been -- been heard, and it's useful that Your Honours have intervened to make that point now as it does give the option, then, in relation to this party producing evidence, that the Court has said it would like to hear, to have more substantiation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Let me ask Mr. Barriot for the last time. Can you give us more specific details on the source of the information, quite apart from the fact that you may have acquired this information through the discharge generally of your duties?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, you put the question again to me, and I'll answer in the same way: I was a military man, I was a colonel in the French army, I was a Blue Helmet in the former Yugoslavia. I was in charge of civilian security. In fact, I took part in all the meetings regarding the fight against terrorism in 1994 and 1995. What else can I tell you? It seems to be obvious. It is obvious I had first-hand information and that I was directly involved in the events. There again, I mean, terrorist attacks I was there. I was on the ground. I experienced them and I intervened on the ground with the wounded but also in the crisis units and the expert groups. I'm one of those who is most published and written about non-conventional techniques and bioterrorism. If that's not enough for you, of course you can then challenge my credibility.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Dr. Barriot, we may be getting closer now, but when you talk about taking part in the all the meetings regarding the fight against terrorism in 1994 and 1995, terrorist attacks, I was there, I was on the ground, are you talking about terrorist attacks in the Balkans?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm speaking about terrorist attacks in France and in the Balkans. In France in 1995, I remind you of the fact that there was this attack against Line B of the RER train in the Saint Michel station, and I just mention in passing that the minister, the French minister of the interior had mentioned some Serbian cause as the source of the attack. So we are in the middle of the problem of terrorist attacks in France with terrorist networks connected to the Algerian GIA and to al Qaeda, to groups that were in Bosnia, attacks and -- where too hastily the Serbs were accused. I think that we are in the very heart of the matter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: We will allow you to proceed on this, Mr. Milosevic. It does go eventually to weight, not admissibility. But the question as to whether we'll be able to attach much value to it is going to be very much in doubt, particularly after cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You mentioned, Colonel Barriot, that the French minister of the interior said, as a matter of fact, when this terrorist attack was launched against Paris, that Serbs may have been involved in it. And what was ultimately established? Who had done it? So here we are referring to this wave of terrorist attacks in France in 1995, in particular to the 25 July 1994 attack on Line B of the RER train.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... this is not relevant to the case at all.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for the Presiding Judge, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: This is not relevant to the case. Ask another question, please.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right. All right. All right. It's not relevant. But it shows what the propaganda at the time was like. Whenever something would happen, they'd say it's got to be the Serbs, and then it would ultimately be established that it wasn't the Serbs. But never mind. Let's move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you have any knowledge regarding the following: To which extent were these terrorist cells embedded in Bosnia-Herzegovina thanks to the hospitality of the Izetbegovic government?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BARRIOT
utterances.text: These terrorist cells were perfectly embedded in Bosnia and Herzegovina. You didn't give me the time. You didn't allow me to speak about the attacks in 1995. I'll mention the second group of terrorists that started working, operating in France in 1996. This Roubaix gang. It was disbanded, dismantled following the attack police station in Lille. It was directed by Christophe Caset. Christophe Caset fought in the Islamist legion in Zenica. There were another two members of the Roubaix gang. Lionel Dumont and Mouloud Bouguela. They, too, fought in Bosnia in the legion of Islamist fighters. They were even detained, gaoled in Bosnia because they raided a petrol station in order to fund their terrorist group. The electronic organiser of Mr. Bouguela showed that he was connected to the Algerian GIA but also to al Qaeda. There is, therefore, an obvious link between the terrorist groups operating in France in 1995 and 1996 and the Islamist fighters especially of Central Bosnia and of the Zenica area. This seems to me a crucial problem, showing that the Bosnian terrorism was feeding outposts towards France, especially in 1995 and 1996. It cannot be ignored as a fact. The problem is that the Western countries realised that the Bosnian terrorism existed and was a problem when they were hit, just as happened for the Americans. It didn't disturb the Americans until they were hit themselves in September 2001. So it shows that these Bosnian forces were at work. Only in September were surveillance teams dispatched. Charitable organisations, Islamic charitable organisation was only then searched. There's also the relief agency. And Islamist charitable organisations were now proved to have supported and funded terrorism, but even after the Dayton agreements, all these structures remained operational and active --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I'm stopping you. Mr. Milosevic, just explain the relevance. Assuming that what the witness is saying is true, what is the relevance of this terrorism to any specific charge?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, we're talking about a series of conclusions which were drawn, deduced, if I can use the term, by the international community, a series of acts for which the Serbs were accused and which were actually perpetrated by such groups in Bosnia-Herzegovina. And not only such groups but by the regular forces of the army too. Of the Muslim army, that is, of Bosnia-Herzegovina, just as --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: In answer to me, then, are you saying that one of the crimes of which you have been charged in the indictment was, in fact, or may have been committed by these terrorists?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know what it is that you are charging me with all here because it's all nebulous, but those terrorists, or even if they were regular forces, they perpetrated a whole series of crimes, both when it comes to sniper fire from -- by which civilians were killed and when it comes to bombs in the Markale 1 and 2 incident, and when it came to the Riclar [phoen] explosion after which sanctions were introduced, although it wasn't the Serbs in Bosnia who perpetrated that but it said in a report filed by the international forces how this actually came about and happened. So we're talking about a series of crimes that were perpetrated in order to accuse the Serbs and demonise them. So it is a far broader context for the demonisation of the Serbs. And it was on the basis of this demonisation of the Serbs that a series of accusations and counts were brought here, including the charges and counts that those people over there are trying to prove here, of course without any evidence and proof.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Kay.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] A series of crimes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Kay, I'm asking you for assistance on this because I think it's going to feature throughout the Defence, how the accused is able to establish the relevance of much of the evidence that he's seeking to lead, particularly when he seeks to lead evidence about Serb suffering, Serb detention, if it is not to be categorised as "you also" evidence, tu quoque evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: In relation to attacks by other parties, and the previous witness referred to being in Sarajevo and being the -- aware of, I'm not sure if she made herself the actual target of, but aware of Muslim attacks on the UN by sniper fire, and we've had the issue in the case concerning the Markale massacre and the challenge by the Defence of the Prosecution expert who indicated that there may be blame on the Bosnian Serb side in relation to that particular incident. So there is, if you like, a continuum of allegation and counter allegation in relation to certain incidents that feature within the indictment. I am aware since the end of the Prosecution case and the ruling under 98 bis that in fact a great deal of the Sarajevo evidence, sniping evidence, was in fact not to be proceeded with further in the trial because there was no evidence adduced about it, so there has been a greater restriction of certain allegations against the accused. It -- in many respects one has to see how this develops and where it goes to and what specific information is eventually available that can support the contentions of the accused --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: But strictly speaking, to be relevant it must relate in a material way to one of the charges in the indictment.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: If it be established that there were forces, if you like, who were committing attacks for which the Serbs were being held responsible and that those are charges within this indictment, then of course the accused is advancing a positive case on such an issue. If that is established. In many respects we have to see where this goes, and where this might be general evidence that the witness is giving, but if there is any specific evidence that's later to flow from the Defence case in relation to charges. One anticipates that he was not an actor in relation to those events but is giving information that was available to him from intelligence sources, and in many respects there has to be a linkage now with what has happened in relation to this witness's evidence with perhaps specific matters within the indictment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: What Mr. Milosevic has to be aware of is that we don't have any interest in your telling your story unless that story is relevant to the indictment. If you want to tell a story, to tell your story, then -- in a manner which is not relevant to the indictment, this is not the forum for it. The evidence that is to be led must relate in a material way to one of the charges. And I am going to be quite strict in that regard and to ask you to explain, when you deal with fact witnesses, how the evidence relates to a specific charge, because that really is the test of relevance. Let us not -- Judge Bonomy.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Kay, one of Mr. Milosevic's points of criticism of your involvement at all in his case has been that you don't know what his case is, and that presupposes that he knows what his case is, and on that basis are the Trial Chamber not entitled to expect him to be able to identify the relevance of any evidence he leads; in other words, identify what charge on the indictment that evidence may be relevant to?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes, of course. And questions may be asked of the litigating party to explain themselves in that way, as the Bench is doing now. I'm using my knowledge and experience of what has gone before in piecing together parts of this with -- I mean, I have had an involvement in these matters, as the Court knows, on many different levels and been able to look at many different things in that time, as to where this evidence is particularly going, looking at the time period that he was in the region of Bosnia as well as the Krajina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I'm simply suggesting that you're perhaps being unduly generous when you say we have to wait and see where the evidence goes, that in fact the accused ought to know when he leads a witness where the evidence is going to go.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes, I understand that. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, Mr. Milosevic, continue.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Robinson, just one comment on my part, very briefly, if I may. We're not dealing here with proving tit for tat or saying, "You did that to us as well." What we're talking about here is showing that the Serbs defended themselves, and that is a substantive difference. You have the facts that this paramilitary formation in Bosnia, the so-called Patriotic League was formed on the 31st of March, 1991, for instance, and that date is celebrated there today now, and that was one year before the war, and that at the beginning of the war they had some 100.000 men under arms, and you have proof of that. And then you go into various details whereas we're exclusively discussing the fact and it is a matter of the Serbs defending themselves, and everything that is being presented here and now shows that the Serbs defended themselves and were defending themselves both in Croatia and Bosnia. That's the essence, the crux of the matter, not you did this to us and tit for tat. Of course, in the conflict that ensues you have crimes committed on all sides but the crux of the matter here is that the Serbs were defending themselves. So we are creating a mosaic here of the different elements about the facts that have otherwise been distorted and erroneously interpreted. But yes, I will try and speed up --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Let me say, Mr. Milosevic, you're on very solid ground there if you can show that the Serbs were defending themselves in relation to a particular charge in the indictment. You're on very, very solid ground there, and I would certainly agree that that evidence is relevant. That's not tu quoque evidence at all. So if in relation to a specific charge in the indictment your answer is it didn't happen the way the Prosecutor said, the Serbs were defending themselves, and in defending themselves 100 Serbs died, that evidence is relevant, certainly relevant. Or a hundred Serbs were detained, that evidence can be led in that way. That evidence is relevant. Yes, continue.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Robinson, you know full well that you had that man there of yours, one of your experts or Mr. Nice's experts, a military expert in fact, and you know full well that what happened, what took place and the things written down in the indictment have nothing to do with me at all. And I am endeavouring to have the truth out about the whole matter. Now, the fact that I have been charged here and counts have been brought against me --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... the case, so proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Colonel Barriot, do you have any knowledge about the links and contacts between the nests of violence and terrorists in Kosovo and the terrorist groups working in Europe?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BARRIOT
utterances.text: Yes. I do have some information about that as far as the links between the terrorist networks operating in Bosnia and those networks connected to the GIA and al Qaeda, which I've mentioned before, also connected with the terrorist networks in Kosovo and Albania, because it's an Albanian and Bosnian terrorist group which is based in Tirana and extends or reaches out to Sarajevo and also has a base in Pristina. So this is a terrorist network which has links with the Algerian GIA and al Qaeda and largely funded thanks to drugs trafficking which crosses the Albanian frontier. And Mr. Geurin Javier [phoen] clearly demonstrated that drug trafficking, which has increased to five million tonnes a year as opposed to 2 million beforehand is something which I'm sure you will get back to. I'd also like to stress the fact that in the north of Albania there are terrorist training camps in the former home of Sali Berisha, the ex-former president of Albania. And all these terrorist training camps in Northern Albania led to frequent intrusions across the border, direction of Kosovo, and in the years 1990 -- 1998 and 1999. I'd also like to stress the fact that we were quite sure that Osama bin Laden was present in the north of Albania from October -- in October 1998 when Richard Holbrooke and Madeleine Albright were supporting the KLA in Kosovo and providing arms to them. So we know full well where these training camps are located, we know how these camps have been funded, we know how they are organised, and clearly we understand there is a link here. Thanks to the Islamic charities - I have mentioned two of these - this is an important factor, relief agency and Saudi High Commission Relief, organisations which organised the entire logistic support of these terrorist networks throughout the Balkans, and I'd like to stress this: That as far as Bosnia is concerned, the SDF, Alija Izetbegovic was coordinating the trafficking and coordinating all these terrorist networks. As early as in 1992 the Islamic fighters arrived in Bosnia, in Sandzak, and we also have proof of the arrival of the Afghan Mujahedin, of the Iranian fighters, and all these Islamic fighters who were supported by Turkey, Iran, Saudi Arabia, Pakistan, or Sudan. So these networks are perfectly well coordinated and very efficient. The major difficulty was that we had to wait for the September 11th attack for people to start looking into it seriously. For instance searches which were conducted in Bosnia which enabled the arrest of ten or so terrorists, six of which were members of the Algerian GIA, Mr. Bensaya Belkassem, who was one of the members of al Qaeda. So I don't know what additional evidence you need. We can ask Mr. Osama bin Laden to sign a paper to clearly state the facts of the matter. I think things are clear enough. I don't think one can question the presence or the organisation of these terrorist networks. The training camps of Terry Bosilja [phoen] were -- remained opened whilst the Stabilisation Force was present in Bosnia, with 10.000 soldiers deployed in the region. That the training camps were not closed down; they could hold the Bosnian nationality, they had false paper, they had drug money, and could go to the training camps, and had money from Islamic charities that was funding them and supporting them. And if you question all of this, I think you question the entire Islamic terrorist groups and entire networks of al Qaeda.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Barriot, as far as your immediate knowledge of concrete events, I'd like to proceed in chronological order and be as efficient as possible, so let's take Krajina and Croatia in 1994 and 1995 first. And I should like to emphasise this, because this is -- there's always a question mark as to whether you know something about previous events or not, but I would like to link this up with the knowledge you have of the previous period which you gained as an officer and UNPROFOR member and must necessarily have had. So first of all could you tell me please whether you, before you arrived in 1994 officially, in your official capacity, and at corresponding official meetings that -- were you informed as a professional and expert about the forerunning events to the actual situation as it was when you arrived?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BARRIOT
utterances.text: Well, I think it's important to establish a distinction between those ideas I might have had before arriving as a Blue Helmet in the former Yugoslavia. I believed in those ideas which had been broadcast by the press, fairly simplistic views, black and white, in other words, the Serbs are the aggressors and the Croats are the people being aggressed. Once I arrived there and I was working as a Blue Helmet and joined the French Glina Battalion and I saw with my own eyes the situation as it stood, and when I was able to hear the Blue Helmets of other nationality, Canadian Blue Helmets, for instance, who had been working in the Medak pocket in 1993, a number of other Canadian soldiers who were based in Sarajevo and other areas, we had meetings, we held meetings within UNPROFOR every day and each soldier, each officer, each military talked about his experience and imparted to us the conclusions they reached. So during this period, I -- while I was in Krajina, I realised that the military were well aware of the situation which had nothing to do which was being described by the press, by the media and by the print press. Would you like me to expand on this? Would you like me to describe the situation as it stood in 1994?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: There's no need. We'll come to that. But we're not talking about the press alone but official positions with respect to the conflicts in the former Yugoslavia. So what you are testifying about is this: That the officers who were on the ground knew full well how the facts stood but that the picture that was presented in public was distorted. Is that what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BARRIOT
utterances.text: Yes. Without any doubt whatsoever that's exactly what I'm saying. And I had stated this in my evidence. The military were analysing the situation which was radically different from what was being broadcast by the media, but they could not express themselves, and they could not have broadcast this. So -- if they were to incur any penalties, and serious penalties, because this was not the general political consensus at the time. But I would like to repeat this: The military, in general terms, had analysed the situation in the same way which has been perfectly described by generals like MacKenzie, also Michael Rose or a number of other French generals. I think that the -- the opinion of the military, I don't think, is a thing which they doubt. They had a very clear picture of the situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Let's try and be very practical. I was just waiting for the interpretation. Let's be practical about this. A moment ago you described the situation and said that you had later on become a representative of Republika Srpska Krajina in France. I assume that you explained to the people in France what was going on during that first year, 1990 and 1991. So on the basis of what were you able to report to them on what was happening in 1990 and 1991 during the course of your work since you were not there, since you hadn't arrived before 1994? How were you able to do that, then?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BARRIOT
utterances.text: Yes. That's quite right. The information I had stemmed from different sources. As we mentioned earlier on, the discussion and briefing sessions which were held by UNPROFOR, because briefing sessions were held on a daily basis, and during these meetings, we outlined the conflict from the beginning.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I apologise for interrupting, but at those meetings you spoke about the conflict since it started. So at how many briefings with the other -- how many briefings did you attend with the other UNPROFOR officers?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BARRIOT
utterances.text: Personally, I took part in ten such briefing sessions. Within UNPROFOR, we outlined the history of the conflict at these meetings, and we anticipated what had happened as early as 1994. I remember during these UNPROFOR meetings things were quite clear, and all the military were saying that the conflict is going to resume in Croatia and more specifically in Krajina, and the Croatian army is going to attack again in the next few months. So the analysis conducted by the military was dead right. They were not only trying to understand what had happened beforehand but they had anticipated on what was actually going to happen a few months down the road. So much for the military sources. But as I was a doctor and, as I told you, canvassed the whole region, the Krajina, the Bihac pocket and Croatia, I met a great number of victims in 1990 and 1991. So I am able to talk about what these people have experienced. And as I was the official representative of the Serbian Republic of Krajina, I was in contact with the authorities of this region, and a lot of my information stemmed from there. Let me remind you also that I have written one of those rare books written on the Serbs of Krajina. For all these reasons, I hope Mr. Nice is not going to question my testimony. I am able to talk about those events which took place in 1990 and 1991, those that preceded my arrival in Krajina. If you have no objection, I shall begin with this first part, the 1990s and 1991, those years in Croatia. I will try to be as brief as possible, but certain things should be told because it would help us to understand what happened afterwards. Now, on the -- when Franjo Tudjman came to power in May of 1990, the HDZ was created and had been created --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Barriot, this method of giving evidence is novel to me. You must answer questions that are put by Mr. Milosevic. So, Mr. Milosevic, he's now going to testify, I understand, about the years 1990, 1991 in Croatia, on the basis of information that he gathered. Please put some questions to him. I don't want to just hear a long narrative from the witness which doesn't proceed in any particular direction.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Of course, fundamentally, Your Honours, is a narrative from this witness based on what he was told by a range of other people of any real value to this Chamber?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, but we do take in hearsay. I say it's a question of the weight to be attached to it, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: What you know about everything that happened from the very outset, from the very beginning of the conflict or, rather, the deployment of UNPROFOR in Krajina, is all of that based on facts that are official facts that were heard at UNPROFOR briefings that you took part in?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BARRIOT
utterances.text: Yes, indeed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: In addition to all the other facts that you compiled. So these are analyses that you had with the UNPROFOR officers. So it implies full competence; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BARRIOT
utterances.text: That's quite right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Tell me now, please, since later on as the representative of Krajina, as you said, you endeavoured to provide objective information in the West, who did you say was responsible for the bloodshed at that time, in the period that you were talking about. Who did you say was responsible for the conflict and on the basis of what?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: This is different from narrating hearsay from entirely anonymous sources. This is now seeking to form a judgement that I dare say is the judgement ultimately for the Court on the basis of anonymous hearsay, and on behalf of the Prosecution we must protest that this has gone quite as far as it should go and these questions should neither be asked nor answered.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: It's not for him to speak to the responsibility. That's a matter ultimately for the Chamber. He can say what he was told. Then it is for us to determine what value, if any, to attach to it.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, please, and quite briefly, without going into any kind of political pre-history, what is the knowledge that you have, since you were an active-duty officer and since you took part in these briefings. What is the knowledge that you have about what happened in 1990 and 1991, in the briefest possible terms?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BARRIOT
utterances.text: Yes, I shall be brief, because the knowledge I have is very clear and is not confusing. For all UNPROFOR officers, it is quite clear that those events started in 1990 and were conducted by the Croat authorities because the Serbs had been set aside. And this was part of the programme of Franjo Tudjman as of 1990 onwards. Franjo Tudjman and the HDZ brought out all the coat of arms and all the insignia of the World War II and glorified Ante Pavelic, introduced Mile Budak's plan, changed street names, replaced the dinar with the kuna and the Ustasha army was established. All of this can be checked out. This can be verified. And there was -- all of this was established by way of symbols, and the tools and instruments were provided. Special units were created by the home affairs ministry or the Jesenje Kise, headed by Tomislav Mercep. Then there were National Guard units which were established, the military police units. A whole series of illegal organisations were set up. Croatia at the time was not independent and was not entitled to have its own army because there was a federal army at the time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, a question. Mr. Milosevic, are you not going to bring evidence from other witnesses about that period in Croatia? Are you not going to bring witnesses who can testify more directly about these events? Because if you are, I mean, why are you bothering to get this from this witness when the evidence is not going to be of much value?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Robinson, taking everything into account, you should bear in mind that at the same time, this witness is an UNPROFOR insider. He is speaking about things that were quite clear, things that UNPROFOR officers in the field had to know about. So there is no doubt that there could have been any kind of confusion. So the confusion that was created was created intentionally, because if it was clear to the witness as it was to other officers what was going on and conclusions were drawn to the contrary, then it is quite clear --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I think you have offered what I consider to be an explanation. He's speaking as an UNPROFOR officer, yes, on the basis of information that he gathered.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Tell me, now, what is your knowledge regarding what happened in 1992 and 1993?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BARRIOT
utterances.text: Just in a very -- in a few words, I'd just like to finish off what I started. In other words, after those of -- instruments of physical repression were established, the constitution was changed and in March of 1992 Pakrac, Plitvice and Borovo Selo attacks, these were physical attacks of the troops of the Ministry of the Interior, levelled against the Serbs, and as soon as -- as early as 1992, Mercep and his ministers were in Vukovar. I think that is very important to stress this, because one tends to cut everything up in different periods, and this is what people do when they talk about this war, and this is not logical any more. Vukovar started in November 1991 -- sorry. Vukovar fell in 1991, and Tomislav Mercep started mistreating people already then. So we can't start talking about historical facts when it suits us. We have to put it into perspective and make sure that the events are consistent. So just what I would like to say is that as far as all UNPROFOR officers are concerned, Serbs in Croatia had been deprived of their constitutional rights and were being attacked physically by the troops of the Ministry of the Interior, which were illegal. So much for those years 1991, 1992. Now, if I'm to talk about 1992, 1993, in 1992 UNPROFOR and the UN Security Council decided to establish protected areas. And if the UN had decided to set up these protection areas, it was because the Serbs had been attacked and it was a matter of protecting them. This is why the Serb protected areas were established. So in those years 1992, 1993, those protected areas, and primarily the Southern sector where I was in 1994, were attacked on several occasions by the Croatian forces and UNPROFOR was unable to protect the people as they had committed to. What comes to mind in particular is the plateau of Miljevac which in June of 1992 was attacked by the Croatian forces, the Ravni Kotor and Maslenica in January 1993 were also attacked by the Croatian forces. Attacks launched against the Medak pocket in September of 1993, and I would like to stress this, with the Medak pocket has been talked a lot about in UNPROFOR circles. There were -- the Canadian observers were on the ground in 1994 in Glina, and the General Janko Bobetko admitted that this operation had been planned, and he wrote this in a book. All the military knew this at the time. Which means that during those years 1992, 1993, on three occasions the UN protected areas which were designed to protect the Serbs were not, and the Serbs were not protected, without UNPROFOR being able to do anything. This is very important. It's very important to emphasise this. As early as 1992, 1993, the UN protected areas were quite clearly being attacked.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
